title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements - Second edition, revised 2025 56 Rev.1 Crop evapotranspiration As global agricultural systems face increasing pressure from climate variability, water scarcity, and the growing demand for food, there is a critical need for updated, science-based tools that support efﬁcient and sustainable water use in agriculture. The original FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 56, published in 1998, set a global standard for computing crop evapotranspiration and estimating crop water requirements. Its methodologies have become integral to irrigation planning, agricultural water management, and policy development worldwide.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: op water requirements. Its methodologies have become integral to irrigation planning, agricultural water management, and policy development worldwide. However, advancements in data science, sensor technology, and climate modeling—coupled with emerging challenges such as prolonged droughts and changing weather patterns—have made it essential to revisit and strengthen the technical foundations of this cornerstone publication. The revised FAO 56 responds directly to this need, integrating modern tools such as remote sensing, IoT applications, and enhanced energy balance methods to improve the precision, relevance, and accessibility of crop water estimation under current and future climate conditions.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ed energy balance methods to improve the precision, relevance, and accessibility of crop water estimation under current and future climate conditions. This updated edition not only builds on the scientiﬁc rigor and widespread adoption of the original guidelines but also introduces practical innovations tailored to regional realities, particularly in water-stressed environments. By reﬁning crop coefﬁcient estimation, optimizing irrigation scheduling, and incorporating adaptive strategies, the revised FAO 56 provides a comprehensive framework for addressing the water–food–climate nexus. This publication will serve as a critical technical reference for governments, development agencies, researchers, and practitioners committed to enhancing water productivity, ensuring food security, and promoting climate-resilient agriculture.

text: xxix Foreword Water management in agriculture is increasingly critical as the world faces escalating challenges from climate change, water scarcity, and the demands of an increasing global population. The FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 56, “Crop Evapotranspiration—Guidelines for Computing Crop Water Requirements”, has been a cornerstone of agricultural water management since its first edition in 1998. The standardization of methodologies and the adoption of the Penman-Monteith ET o equation for computing the reference evapotranspiration and then estimating crop evapotranspiration enabled agronomists, researchers, policymakers, and farmers to effectively manage water resources, optimize irrigation practices, and promote sustainable agricultural systems. Its influence is globally reflected in thousands of citations and numerous studies validating its overall accuracy.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: sustainable agricultural systems. Its influence is globally reflected in thousands of citations and numerous studies validating its overall accuracy. In response to significant progress in both science and technology over the past two decades, FAO, in collaboration with key partners, has revised these guidelines. The revamped version not only reaffirms the value of the original guidelines but also integrates cutting-edge techniques such as remote sensing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and improved energy balance methods. These tools enhance the accuracy and applicability of the methods included in the guidelines, addressing the dynamic and complex needs of today’s agricultural systems. Moreover, the new version includes new approaches and datasets, making it adaptable to diverse regional conditions, especially in arid and semi-arid areas.

The revised guidelines are also key for addressing the pressing challenges posed by climate change. Rising temperatures and shifting precipitation patterns reinforce the need for more precise information on crop water requirements and more efficient water use in agriculture. This revamped version introduces refined methodologies for optimizing water allocation, incorporating water-saving strategies, and advancing crop coefficient estimation and irrigation scheduling. These enhancements enable stakeholders to tailor their irrigation practices to local conditions, preserve water, and support food security while minimizing environmental impacts.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: 1 1. Introduction to evapotranspiration Introduction to evapotranspiration This chapter introduces the evapotranspiration process and explains the concepts of and the differences between reference crop evapotranspiration (ET o) and crop evapotranspiration under standard conditions (ET c) and various management and environmental conditions (ETc act). It examines the factors that affect evapotranspiration, the units in which it is normally expressed and the way in which it can be determined. It also describes the field methods used to determine the ETc act, as well as the main remote sensing ET methods. 1.1 EVAPOTRANSPIRATION PROCESS The combination of two separate processes whereby water is transferred to the atmosphere, on the one hand from the soil surface by evaporation and, on the other hand, from the crop by transpiration, is referred to as evapotranspiration (ET).

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: n the one hand from the soil surface by evaporation and, on the other hand, from the crop by transpiration, is referred to as evapotranspiration (ET). 1.1.1 Evaporation Evaporation is the process whereby liquid water is converted to water vapour (vaporization) and removed from the evaporating surface (vapour removal). Water evaporates from a variety of surfaces, such as lakes, rivers, pavements, soils and vegetation. Energy is required to change the state of the molecules of water from liquid to vapour. Direct solar radiation and, to a lesser extent, the ambient temperature of the air provide this energy. The driving force to remove water vapour from the evaporating surface is the difference between the water vapour pressure at the evaporating surface and that of the surrounding atmosphere.

text: 6 Crop evapotranspiration 1.4 EVAPOTRANSPIRATION CONCEPTS Distinctions are made (Figure 1.4) between reference crop evapotranspiration (ET o), crop evapotranspiration under standard conditions (ET c) and crop evapotranspiration under non-standard conditions, i.e. actual conditions (ET c act ). ET o is a climatic parameter expressing the evaporation power of the atmosphere. ET c refers to the evapotranspiration from excellently managed and disease-free, large, well-watered fields that achieve full production under the given climatic conditions. Due to suboptimal crop management and environmental constraints that affect crop growth and yield and any presence of water stress, evapotranspiration may be limited, and therefore the actual ETc under non-standard conditions, ETc act, requires a correction.

The reference surface is a hypothetical grass reference crop with specific characteristics. The use of other denominations and terms such as potential ET is strongly discouraged due to ambiguities in their definitions. The concept of reference evapotranspiration was introduced to study the evaporative demand of the atmosphere independent of crop type, crop development and management practices. As water is abundantly available at the reference evapotranspiring surface, soil factors do not affect ETo.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: crop development and management practices. As water is abundantly available at the reference evapotranspiring surface, soil factors do not affect ETo. Relating ETo to a specific surface provides a reference to which ET from other surfaces can be related. It obviates the need to define a separate ET equation or level for each crop and stage of growth. ET o values measured or calculated at different locations or in different seasons are comparable as they refer to the ET from the same reference surface. The only factors affecting ET o are climatic parameters. Consequently, ET o is a climatic parameter and must be computed from weather data. ET o expresses the evaporating power of the atmosphere at a specific location and time of the year and does not consider crop characteristics and soil factors.

Specific devices and accurate measurements of various physical parameters include the soil water balance in lysimeters or the field, as well as the energy balance performed on the ground or through remote sensing, and are required to determine evapotranspiration. The methods are commonly expensive, demanding in terms of accuracy of measurements and can only be fully exploited by well-trained research personnel. Although the methods are inappropriate for routine measurements, they remain important for the evaluation of ET estimates obtained by more indirect methods.

However, in many instances, understanding the underlying physics of turbulence and heat, water and energy transfer that govern the measurement is crucial to avoid subtle biases and mistakes that will compromise the accuracy of the data. For the purpose of producing representative and reliable data, the deployment of equilibrium air-boundary layer systems, such as eddy covariance, the Bowen ratio, and scintillometers, must abide by fetch requirements and minimum equipment heights.

Therefore, the evapotranspiration process is governed by energy exchange at the vegetation surface and is limited by the amount of energy available. Because of this limitation, it is possible to estimate the evapotranspiration rate by applying the principle of energy conservation. The energy arriving at the surface must equal the energy leaving the surface for the same period. The energy leaving the surface includes the energy consumed by the λET process. The λ variable represents the latent heat of vaporization, described earlier, that is required per unit of ET.

The use of the word “latent” means that this energy is “hidden” in the vapour that is produced by the ET. All primary fluxes of energy should be considered when deriving an energy balance equation. The equation for an evaporating surface can be written as: Rn - G - λET - H = 0 (1.1) where Rn is the net radiation, H is the sensible heat flux, G is the soil heat flux and λET is the latent heat flux. The various terms can be either positive or negative. Positive Rn supplies energy to the surface and positive G, λET and H remove energy from the surface (Figure 1.5).

The equation is restricted to the four components: Rn, λET, H and G. Other energy terms, such as heat stored or released in the plant, or the energy used in metabolic activities and photosynthesis, are not considered. These terms account for only a small fraction of the daily net radiation and can be considered negligible when compared with the other four components. The latent heat flux (λ ET) representing the evapotranspiration fraction can be derived from the energy balance equation if all other components are known. Net radiation (R n) and soil heat fluxes (G) can be measured or estimated from climatic parameters. Measurements of the sensible heat (H) are however complex and cannot be easily obtained.

H requires accurate measurement of temperature gradients above the surface. Another method for estimating evapotranspiration is using a mass transfer method. This approach considers the vertical movement of small parcels of air (eddies) above a large homogeneous surface. The eddies transport material (water vapour) and energy (heat and momentum) from and towards the evaporating surface. By assuming steady state conditions and that the eddy transfer coefficients for water vapour are proportional to those for heat and momentum, the evapotranspiration rate can be computed from the vertical gradients of air temperature and water vapour above the surface via the Bowen Ratio Energy Balance (BREB).

Eddy covariance (EC) systems are often used for crop ET monitoring due to their relative simplicity of setup, moderate sensor prices and, depending on the equipment settings, the ability to simultaneously measure H, λET and CO2 fluxes. The concept of eddy covariance (also known as eddy correlation) refers to the statistical covariance between vertical fluxes of vapour or sensible heat within the upward and downward legs of turbulent eddies. Quick response sensors must be used to make high speed measurements of air temperature (T), vertical wind velocity (w), and mean vapour pressure (e) or mean specific humidity (q), normally at frequencies of 5-20 Hz (5-20 times per second), typically at 10 Hz.

Additionally, ET can be calculated as a residual from the energy balance equation as λET = R n – G – H, which has the advantage of eliminating the need to measure q, although it does require accurate measurements of R n and G. A large number of corrections are required with the EC procedure, and there is a variety of software available for EC flux processing. Many studies have reported a lack of energy balance closure for EC data since the sum of the measured turbulent fluxes (H + λET) usually underestimates the measured available energy (R n − G). This underestimation can often be as large as 30 percent.

A scintillometer is an optical device that measures small fluctuations in the refractive index of air caused by temperature, humidity, and pressure induced variations in density. The most common scintillometers measure sensible heat flux, H, by relating the structure parameter to a temperature parameter and the Monin-Obukhov stability parameters. A scintillometer system for measuring sensible heat flux consists of an optical transmitter and a receiver at the ends of an atmospheric propagation path.

To obtain λET, measurements of R n and G are needed, which can be problematic and biased in heterogeneous and sparse vegetation systems. Scintillometers are relatively simple to operate and maintain. Their cost can equal or exceed those of BREB and EC systems. A distinct advantage of scintillometry is the ability to derive sensible heat flux that is integrated over a long transect, up to several km in length. This integration is especially useful for measuring H over complex natural vegetation where spatial variation can have scales of hundreds of meters.

In precision weighing lysimeters, where the water loss is directly measured by measuring the change of mass of the complete system, evapotranspiration can be obtained with an accuracy of a few hundredths of a millimetre, and small time periods such as an hour or even less can be considered. In non-weighing drainage lysimeters, the evapotranspiration for a given time period is determined by deducting the drainage water, collected at the bottom of the lysimeters, from the total water input. Non-weighing drainage lysimeters can generally only provide ET information at a weekly or longer time scale.

On the contrary, static water table lysimeters can be very accurate and provide for daily time step or longer measurements since ET corresponds to the amount of water transferred during the considered time period from the groundwater. These lysimeters are of particular interest for studies referring to the contribution of the groundwater to the crop under study. They are commonly used to define the target depth of the water table, or when the groundwater is saline. Many studies have used lysimeter ET measurements for evaluation, calibration and validation of different ET approaches. However, lysimeter measurements are very sensitive to environmental aspects, which are often not well interpreted or even taken into account.

The systems introduce a small source of heat into the trunk or branch of a plant and estimate the flow of water in the xylem by either measuring the velocity of a heat pulse carried away from the heat source in the transpiration stream or by the dissipation of heat energy in the stem due to convection in the transpiration stream. These methods do not measure the direct evaporation component of ET, but only the plant transpiration component. This can be an advantage if the goal is to measure plant water use, but is a disadvantage if the goal is to estimate total ET over an extended heterogeneous surface. Three main methods can be employed.

Literature suggests that no one set of theory and instrumentation is applicable to all sizes or species of trees. Heat pulse velocity measurements can determine transpiration in forests and orchards, where the sensors can be applied to any woody stem larger than about 40 mm in diameter. The system is inexpensive, easy to install, and suited to automated data collection. The most commonly used correction method is the compensation heat pulse method. The method may require a knowledge of the wood anatomy of the species being measured to determine sapwood area. The Granier heat dissipation method is suited to transpiration measurements in trees, and it involves inserting a heating needle into the sapwood layer of a large trunk or branch.

Heat is applied at a constant rate rather than as a pulse. Different calibration coefficients may be needed for each tree species and the method assumes that sap flow is radially uniform around the trunk. The tissue heat balance method is the most direct sap flux method with the fewest assumptions. It involves wrapping a heating wire around an entire branch segment and measuring conductive heat losses upstream, downstream and radially away from the heat source by thermocouples referenced to the temperature at the heating wire. The energy balance is conducted on the entire stem segment so that no knowledge of the xylem anatomy or area of conducting sapwood is needed.

The estimation of ET using a vegetation index (VI) is possible due to the generally close correspondence between vegetation amount and transpiration, where, as vegetation cover increases, leaf area increases, and the relative rate of transpiration increases. Generally, the estimation of ET is made using the Kc act ETo approach where the value for K c act is estimated from the VI. The VI is usually updated over time using satellite or drone imagery. Because the K c act from VI represents the transpiration component, challenges with VI-based methods include estimating evaporation from bare soil associated with precipitation and irrigation events.

Under conditions of long periods of water stress, vegetation growth is expected to be less and therefore the VI may be less. However, during conditions of short periods of water stress, the VI may appear to be at unstressed levels even though the ET may decline due to partial or full closure of stomates. Remote sensing surface energy balance (RSSEB) methods take advantage of the physical fact that conversion of liquid water to the vapour form requires very substantial amounts of energy. This conversion of liquid to vapour during the evaporation process involves the same physical requirements whether the process is the transpiration of water from inside a plant leaf or the evaporation of water from a wet soil surface. Approximately 2.4 million Joules (2.4 megajoules) of energy are required to evaporate one kilogram of water at room temperature.

The energy source can be in the form of heat energy from the surrounding air (this is termed “sensible heat” since it can be sensed with a thermometer), and the energy source also includes the radiant energy from the sun and atmosphere in the form of photons contacting the evaporating surface. Energy from photons is converted into freeing water molecules from a liquid to vapour state. The surface energy balance determination of ETc act is usually conducted using Equation 1.1. Some RSSEB models, for example, the METRIC model, utilize reference ET to establish upper limits on the estimated ET c act. 1.5.7 ET computed from meteorological data Owing to the difficulty of obtaining accurate field measurements, ET is commonly computed from weather data.

A large number of empirical or semi-empirical equations have been developed for assessing crop or reference crop evapotranspiration from meteorological data. Some of the methods are only valid under specific climatic and agronomic conditions and cannot be applied under conditions different from those under which they were originally developed. Numerous researchers have analyzed the performance of the various calculation methods for different locations. As a result of an Expert Consultation held in May 1990, the FAO Penman-Monteith ET o method is recommended as the standard method for the definition and computation of the grass reference evapotranspiration (ETo).

The FAO PenmanMonteith method is recommended as the sole standard ET o method for determining reference evapotranspiration. The method, its derivation, the required meteorological data and reference weather site conditions, and the corresponding definition of the reference surface are described in this chapter. Also included is the correction of data collected over non-reference weather sites and the application of Quality Assurance and Quality Control (QAQC) to measured meteorological data.

Relationships were often subject to rigorous local calibrations and have proved to have limited global validity. Testing the accuracy of ET methods under a new set of conditions is laborious, time-consuming and costly, and yet evapotranspiration data are frequently needed at short notice for project planning or irrigation scheduling design. To meet this need, guidelines were developed and published in the FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 24 “Crop water requirements”.

To accommodate users with different data availability, four methods were presented to calculate the reference crop evapotranspiration (ET o): the BlaneyCriddle, radiation, modified Penman and pan evaporation methods. The modified Penman method was considered to offer the best results with a minimum possible error in relation to a living grass reference crop. It was expected that the pan method would give acceptable estimates, depending on the location of the pan. The radiation method was suggested in FAO Paper No. 24 for areas where available climatic data include measured air temperature and sunshine, cloudiness or radiation, but not measured wind speed and air humidity.

These climatic methods to calculate ET o were all calibrated for ten-day or monthly calculations, not for daily or hourly calculations. The Blaney-Criddle method was recommended for periods of one month or longer. For the pan method, it was suggested that calculations should be done for periods of ten days or longer. The ASCE study analyzed the performance of 20 different methods, using detailed procedures to assess the validity of the methods compared to a set of carefully screened lysimeter data from 11 international locations with a broad range of climatic conditions. The study proved very revealing and showed the widely varying performance of the methods under different climatic conditions. In a parallel study commissioned by the European Community, a consortium of European research institutes evaluated the performance of various evapotranspiration methods using data from different lysimeter studies in Europe.

The comparative studies may be summarized as follows: • The semi-empirical Penman methods may require local calibration of the wind function to achieve satisfactory results. • The radiation methods show good results in humid climates where the aerodynamic term is relatively small, but performance in arid conditions is erratic and tends to underestimate evapotranspiration. • Temperature methods remain empirical and require local calibration in order to achieve satisfactory results.

FAO Penman-Monteith ETo equation 2.2 FORMULATION OF THE PENMAN-MONTEITH EQUATION 2.2.1 Penman-Monteith combination equation In 1948, Penman combined the energy balance with the mass transfer method and derived an equation to compute the evaporation from an open water surface from standard climatological records of sunshine, temperature, air humidity and wind speed. This so-called combination method was further developed by many researchers, including Monteith in 1965, and was extended to cropped surfaces by introducing resistance factors. The resistance nomenclature distinguishes between aerodynamic resistance and surface resistance factors (Figure 2.1). The surface resistance parameters are often combined into one parameter, the “bulk” surface resistance parameter, which operates in series with the aerodynamic resistance.

The surface resistance, r s, describes the resistance of vapour flow through stomata openings, total leaf area and soil surface. The aerodynamic resistance, r a, describes the resistance to vapour and heat flow from the vegetation upward and involves friction from air flowing over vegetative surfaces (Figure 2.1). Although the exchange process in a vegetation layer is too complex to be fully described by the two resistance factors, good correlations can be obtained between measured and calculated evapotranspiration rates, especially for a uniform grass reference surface.

The Leaf Area Index (LAI), a dimensionless quantity, is the leaf area (upper side only) per unit area of soil below it. It is expressed as m 2 leaf area per m 2 ground area. The active LAI is the index of the leaf area that actively contributes to surface heat and vapour transfer. It is generally the upper, sunlit portion of a dense canopy. The LAI values for various crops differ widely but values of 3 to 5 are common for many mature crops. Evapotranspiration rates of the various crops are related to the evapotranspiration rate from the reference surface (ETo) by means of crop coefficients. In the past, an open water surface has been proposed as a reference surface.

However, the differences in aerodynamic, vegetation control and radiation characteristics present a strong challenge in relating ET to measurements of free water evaporation. Relating ETo to a specific crop has the advantage of incorporating the biological and physical processes involved in ET from cropped surfaces. Grass, together with alfalfa, is a well-studied crop regarding its aerodynamic and surface characteristics and is accepted worldwide as a reference surface. Because the resistance to diffusion of vapour strongly depends on crop height, ground cover, LAI and soil moisture conditions, the characteristics of the reference crop should be well

text: 28 Crop evapotranspiration defined and fixed. Changes in crop height result in variations in the roughness and LAI. Consequently, the associated canopy and aerodynamic resistances will vary appreciably with time. Moreover, water stress and the degree of ground cover have an effect on the resistances and also on the albedo. To avoid problems of local calibration which would require demanding and expensive studies, a hypothetical grass reference has been selected with well-defined properties. Difficulties with a living grass reference result from the fact that the grass variety and morphology can significantly affect the evapotranspiration rate, especially during peak water use. Large differences may exist between warm-season and cool-season grass types. Cool-season grasses have a lower degree of stomatal control and hence higher rates of evapotranspiration.

It is important, when comparing the FAO-PM ET o equation to ET o measurements, that the full Penman-Monteith equation (Equation 2.1) and associated equations for ra and r s (Equations 2.2 and 2.3) must be used to enable accounting for variation in ET due to variation in height of the grass measured.

In the crop coefficient approach, differences in the crop canopy and aerodynamic resistance relative to the hypothetical reference crop are accounted for within the crop coefficient. The K c factor serves as an aggregation of the physical and physiological differences between crops and the reference definition. 2.4.2 Impacts of advection Many irrigated areas around the globe are located in semiarid and arid regions where irrigated agriculture is downwind of extensive regions of dryness. The upwind dry regions, through surface heating, increase air temperature and dryness to the overlying air mass.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: wind of extensive regions of dryness. The upwind dry regions, through surface heating, increase air temperature and dryness to the overlying air mass. Two types of advection can exist, local advection and regional advection, where advection is defined as the transport of warmer, drier air onto an irrigated surface. When warmer, drier air is transported onto an irrigated surface, it increases the air temperature and decreases the humidity above the irrigated surface as compared to what would occur in the absence of the advection. The advection will tend to increase the corresponding ET rate. Local advection Local advection occurs when a nearby dry field generates warmer air directly upwind of an adjacent irrigated field. That warmer air can create an increase in ET at the edges of the downwind irrigated field and into the field for tens of meters.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: cent irrigated field. That warmer air can create an increase in ET at the edges of the downwind irrigated field and into the field for tens of meters. After the establishment of a new equilibrium boundary layer (EBL) some tens of meters into the irrigated field, the effects of the local advection are reduced. The definition for ET o given earlier in this chapter describes ET o as the ET from an extensive surface of well-watered, clipped grass. The extensive surface is specified so that the impacts of local advection on the edges of a field are made small in proportion to the total field ET, and so that weather measurements are less influenced by local advection. The ET o estimate is, thereby, intended to represent the basis for the ET produced from the majority of a medium to large, irrigated field. That ET is calculated as Kc ETo.

text: thereby, intended to represent the basis for the ET produced from the majority of a medium to large, irrigated field. That ET is calculated as Kc ETo. In other words, the ET o estimate represents ET that occurs for the average well-watered field when surrounded by other agricultural fields that may have low or high amounts of vegetated cover at various times during the growing season. For this reason, it is mandatory that weather stations are set up under reference conditions, i.e. over a well-watered grass field surrounded by other agricultural fields.

text: 34 Crop evapotranspiration Regional advection Contrary to the impact of local advection, irrigated areas that are downwind of large areas of dryness, such as in semiarid and arid climates, are influenced by regional advection. Regional advection transports warmer and drier air from an arid planetary boundary layer toward an irrigated surface. The transport of warmer and drier air affects all fields of an irrigated area and is made possible by turbulent eddy transfer. The regional advection impacts the air temperature and humidity gradients above the irrigated surface, effectively increasing the air temperature and reducing the humidity at the 2 m height. These changes increase ET from the irrigated surface.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: surface, effectively increasing the air temperature and reducing the humidity at the 2 m height. These changes increase ET from the irrigated surface. The changes in gradients over the irrigated fields are assumed to be similar to those experienced at a reference weather station that has a well-watered, transpiring surface and is located in a similar environment. In those situations, the FAO Penman-Monteith equation responds to the impacted temperature and humidity gradients established by the weather data and produces higher ET o. That higher ET o, in turn, corresponds to the higher ET that occurs from well-watered fields under regional advection. This phenomenon is common to irrigated fields in arid and semiarid regions and is accurately treated by the FAO Penman-Monteith ETo equation due to its use of solar radiation, air temperature, air humidity and wind speed measurements.

text: 36 Crop evapotranspiration collected over transpiring surfaces. The assumptions in the combination equation, including the calculation of the slope of the vapour pressure curve (∆) using air temperature, require that the temperature of the surface be similar to the air temperature, or within a few degrees. This is usually the case for the reference ETo because ET from a well-watered grassed surface consumes most of the energy available from R n and G, so that sensible heat, H, is small. A small value for H means that differences between surface temperature and air temperature are also small. Vapour transport from a transpiring surface increases the actual vapour pressure of the air for several meters above the surface and cools the air temperature.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ansport from a transpiring surface increases the actual vapour pressure of the air for several meters above the surface and cools the air temperature. This is in contrast to a dry, non-transpiring surface, where heating of the surface adds substantial heat to the air above the surface, but no vapour. The FAO-PM ET o equation requires that the near-surface boundary layer that resides for several meters above the surface behaves as that over a transpiring surface where the air temperature is cooled, and vapour pressure is increased. These expectations carry into the estimation of ∆ using air temperature, the calculation of saturation and actual vapour pressure and net radiation. These calculations all utilize the measured air temperature and vapour pressure values.

Applying the combination equation using high temperature and low vapour pressure measured over a non-transpiring surface confuses the equation by instructing it to estimate the ET rate that would be required to occur in spite of high air temperature and low vapour pressure over a transpiring surface. This causes the combination equation to function under an unrealistic and perhaps even impossible situation. This impossible situation must be mitigated by limiting weather data sets to those that are collected over large, well-watered surfaces.

A correction is therefore required to bring temperature and humidity data sets closer to those that would have been measured under reference conditions. Air temperatures decrease during night-time by evaporative cooling when vapour pressure deficit (VPD) is positive and due to surface cooling caused by the emission of long-wave radiation. For reference conditions, simple relationships can be used to assess whether weather data adhere to reference ET conditions and to replace measured humidity data when the data have not been collected under reference ET conditions. For non-reference weather sites and data sets, soil moisture and/or vegetation limitations cause the ET of the site to be substantially less than ET o. As a result, T min may remain well above the reported T dew.

One cause of this phenomenon is the large “reservoir” of sensible heat created during daytime in the atmosphere over an arid region that is transferred towards the dry surface during the night, reducing the effect of cooling by long wave radiation. This surface warming is sustained by the lack of evaporative cooling during nighttime due to the lack of soil moisture at a non-reference site. The result is the air temperature and T dew measurements that are uncharacteristic of a transpiring reference site and that provide the FAO-PM equation with a wrong idea of the underlying ETo. This phenomenon can be observed in Figure 2.4.

text: 38 Crop evapotranspiration In Figure 2.4, monthly means for T min − Tdew are plotted for weather stations operated by the national governments of two countries, Sudan and the United States. The data are plotted against the monthly ratios of precipitation to reference ET o. The P/ETo ratios indicate the availability of soil water to support reference (well-watered) conditions during any particular month in the absence of irrigation. As illustrated by the data, Tmin approaches Tdew for nearly all stations when the ratio P/ET o approaches and exceeds 1.0. This indicates that P is sufficient to supply potential ET rates and to cool and humidify near-surface air. When P/ETo < 1.0, then the aridity of the area causes heating and reduces humidification, and T min thereby may substantially exceed measured T dew.

text: 39 2. FAO Penman-Monteith ETo equation 2.5.1 Adjustments to weather daily data collected over dry surfaces Researchers, hydrologists and engineers have long recognized the impact of local aridity on near-surface weather measurements and the lack of synchronization and equilibrium of those measurements with that expected to occur over evaporating surfaces associated with irrigated agriculture. The lack of synchronization and equilibrium creates a consequent incongruence within ET o equations such as the standardized FAO-PM ETo as was described in a previous section. Empirical methods have been developed to adjust arid air temperature downward or to adjust arid vapour pressure upward. Some of the more simple methods are described in this section.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: loped to adjust arid air temperature downward or to adjust arid vapour pressure upward. Some of the more simple methods are described in this section. These empirical approaches generally employ linear adjustments based on observed differences between weather data collected from close-by irrigated and non-irrigated locations or by differences between daily minimum air temperature (Tmin) and daily average dewpoint temperature (Tdew). The objective of the adjustments is to produce a corrected weather data set that best reflects weather conditions to be obtained in a well-watered, reference-type environment. These are the data expected by the standardized FAO-PM ETo equation. The following sections describe two procedures for recognizing and correcting nonreference weather data prior to its use to calculate ET o.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: equation. The following sections describe two procedures for recognizing and correcting nonreference weather data prior to its use to calculate ET o. The second procedure adjusts both air temperature and dewpoint temperature whereas the first procedure is even simpler and adjusts dewpoint temperature data only. Both procedures can produce very helpful adjustments that account for the aridity of a weather station site and the data collected, and help to bring the data into synchronization with the reference surface. A third type of procedure for adjusting air temperature, humidity and even wind speed data utilizes a more theoretical boundary layer profile theory. These procedures are still in their infancy, but may become more commonly used in the future due to their more physical basis and ability to automatically identify the extent of adjustments needed.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: t may become more commonly used in the future due to their more physical basis and ability to automatically identify the extent of adjustments needed. 2.5.2 Adjustment to Tdew or ea A simple, yet relatively effective approach to correct weather data collected in a nonreference setting is to retain the measured air temperature data with no adjustment, but to abandon the use of all collected humidity data (Tdew, ea or RH). Instead, replacement humidity data are synthesized to better describe conditions of a reference (wellwatered) environment. The synthesized humidity data set works with the original reported air temperature data to produce a VPD, (es − ea) that is expected to occur in a reference weather station environment.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: orks with the original reported air temperature data to produce a VPD, (es − ea) that is expected to occur in a reference weather station environment. An estimate of actual vapour pressure, e a, can be obtained by assuming that the daily average dewpoint temperature (T dew) is near the daily minimum temperature (T min). This implicitly assumes that at sunrise, when the air temperature is close to T min, that the near-surface air over a well-watered, transpiring surface has cooled, so that it is nearly saturated with water vapour, and the relative humidity is nearly 100 percent. The relationship Tdew ≈ Tmin holds for locations in humid climates and where the cover crop of the station is well watered. However, particularly for arid regions, the air might not be saturated when its temperature is at its minimum due to the entrainment of dry air from above the irrigated area.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: r arid regions, the air might not be saturated when its temperature is at its minimum due to the entrainment of dry air from above the irrigated area. Hence, T min might remain greater than T dew and a further calibration is then recommended to estimate dewpoint temperature. In these situations, T dew may be estimated from T min using subtractive correction factors, a T, that vary with the general aridity of the surrounding region unless the weather station is cropped with irrigated green grass. Thus, a general approach is: Tdew = Tmin - aT (2.6)

The upper limit 6 ºC of the aT values for hyper-arid regions is to be applied only under very stringent site aridity conditions. The UNEP Aridity Index describes the general aridity of the region. The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) aridity index AI is defined by the ratio between the long term means of annual precipitation (P, mm) and the Thornthwaite (1948) annual climatic evaporation index (CEITH, mm) (Box 2.4 and Example 2.1).

It is noted that the use of the T dew = Tmin–aT (Equation 2.6) adjustment may produce a slight upward or downward bias in computed net radiation (R n). The adjustment to ea when Tmin is impacted by station aridity inflates e a above levels expected for reference conditions. This error in e a causes incoming atmospheric long-wave radiation to be overestimated, but the elevated T from using arid data causes outgoing long-wave radiation to be overestimated. These two impacts tend to cancel one another. One may expect up to 1 to 3% under- or overestimation in R n.

The qualified stations should have high integrity humidity and air temperature data as well as be located in extensive well-watered environments. Despite being more laborious, the determination of aT can be made on a monthly basis to capture any seasonality associated with the Tdew vs. T min relationship.

As a consequence, a more accurate estimate for ET o should result than if the actual measurement of Tdew from the arid weather setting had been used with no correction. Thus, when humidity data are adjusted using Tdew = Tmin − aT, no further adjustment is generally needed to the air temperature data set to account for the effects of the aridity of the weather measurement site.

LDAS systems are programmed to electronically assimilate weather data collected from select weather sites around the globe and to couple those data with land process (soil and vegetation water balance) models and with atmospheric models to extend the point data and to create gridded weather data sets that are generally traceable to the original point measurements. Gridded weather data products are made available for the globe from a number of sources including the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) and the European Satellite Applications Facility on Land Surface Analysis (LSA-SAF) framework.

The LSA-SAF framework produces an ET o estimate using a modified Makkink equation using solar radiation derived from the European Meteosat Second Generation (MSG) satellite system. In the USA, gridded weather data sets are produced by NOAA, NASA and NCEP. Many of the gridded weather data sets include 50-year or longer time periods and have spatial resolutions of 1/6 to 1/8 degree (~ 9 km x 9 km to 12 km x 12 km) but some gridded data sets have resolutions as large as 50 km. Time resolutions range from one hour to one day. Many gridded weather data sets contain daily precipitation, solar radiation, and near surface temperature and humidity (at ~2 or 3 m reference height), and wind speed often at ~10 m reference height.

T dew (mm h-1) Reference ETo (mm h-1) 3 hour NARR Source: Authors’ own elaboration 2.6 QUALITY ASSURANCE AND QUALITY CONTROL (QAQC) OF WEATHER DATA Estimates of reference evapotranspiration (ET o) are no better than weather data upon which they are based. Assessments of weather data integrity and quality need to be conducted before data are utilized in ETo equations. Corrections to the data should be made to account for poor sensor calibration, poor maintenance or for a poor weather station environment. Some statistics-based corrections for completion of data sets and for for testing and correction of data sets for homogeneity are described in Annex 3.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ome statistics-based corrections for completion of data sets and for for testing and correction of data sets for homogeneity are described in Annex 3. A cautionary statement in data analysis and application is that “having no data is often better than having bad data.” Bad data refers to data that are substantially biased or are faulty, or are not representative of a well-watered environment. When one has no data, one can look to regional weather or ET data summaries for information that might be useful to represent conditions within the local area. In the case of “bad” weather data,

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: 52 Crop evapotranspiration the ETo procedures of these guidelines will produce faulty estimates of ETo and ETc. The result is the application of evapotranspiration data or evapotranspiration calculations to irrigation water management, to water resources operations, or to irrigation and water resources systems design that can cause greater economic and hydrologic problems than if only reasonable estimates or even “textbook” values for ET c had been used instead. Humanity can be worse off with erroneous data than with no data at all. This statement also applies to the measurements of evapotranspiration that have been used to develop or calibrate reference ET equations or to determine crop coefficients. This section presents guidelines to be used to calculate both expected ranges for weather data measurements and also means to assess integrity of data that fall within the ranges.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: nes to be used to calculate both expected ranges for weather data measurements and also means to assess integrity of data that fall within the ranges. 2.6.1 Solar radiation using clear sky comparisons Pyranometer operation and calibration accuracy should be evaluated for a particular weather location by plotting hourly or daily readings of solar radiation (R s) against computed theoretical short-wave radiation that is expected to occur under clear sky conditions (R so). R so can be computed for any day or hour using Equation 3.35 of Chapter 3 along with calculated R a. The theoretical R so should be expected to plot as an upper envelope of measured R s. Pyranometers that measure solar radiation can be substantially impacted by a drift in the sensor calibration caused by aging or film or dust on the sensor. Pyranometers can also be affected by a lack of level for the sensor.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: a drift in the sensor calibration caused by aging or film or dust on the sensor. Pyranometers can also be affected by a lack of level for the sensor. Other error in R s data can occur from the use of an incorrect calibration factor to convert millivolts of pyranometer signal into radiation units. In many situations, faulty R s data can be corrected by multiplying by a derived coefficient that is determined using the R so values. A simple linear multiplier is often adequate when the problem with sensor reporting is caused by calibration or dirtiness of the sensor. When making corrections, a constant multiplier is recommended to be applied to all data measurements during a specific period under the assumption that the pyranometer malfunction or improper calibration is relatively constant from day to day. Therefore, measured R n data can be plotted against R n data that have been estimated using the equations that are based on measured R s, air temperature and vapour pressure. The value for albedo (α) used in the R n estimating equation should represent conditions of the surface beneath the radiometer. If measured values for R n consistently deviate from estimated values by more than 3-5 percent, then the calibration or operation of the R n device (net radiometer) should be scrutinized.

One should always scan wind records for the presence of consistently constant values occurring during periods of low wind speed. For electronic instruments, these recordings may represent a numerical “offset” in the anemometer calibration equation. The presence of these constant and consistent offsets in the data set indicates either the presence of exceptionally calm conditions (wind speeds less than about 0.5 m s-1 during the entire sampling period, which is rare) or malfunctioning of the wind speed sensor due to electrical shorting or perhaps due to fatigue of bearings. These problems may not be noticed by the station operator.

When possible, a second anemometer of the same design, but with fresh bearings, should be placed at the weather location for a three- or four-day period at least once each year, and recordings compared with the permanent instrument. Variations between recordings can signal a need to replace bearings, switches, or other parts. If a second data logger is used to record the temporary anemometer, one should be careful to synchronize data logger clocks. Also, one should be careful that anemometers do not interfere with one another’s wind stream. Comparisons of wind speed data can be made between two nearby stations using a double mass balance or other statistical method as described in Annex 3.

text: 63 3. Meteorological variables and parameters Meteorological variables and parameters The methods for calculating evapotranspiration from meteorological data require climatological inputs and physical parameters. Some data are measured directly at weather stations. Other parameters are related to commonly measured data and can be derived with the help of a direct or empirical relationship. This chapter discusses the source, measurement and computation of all data required for the calculation of the reference evapotranspiration (ET o) by means of the FAO Penman-Monteith method. Different examples illustrate the various calculation procedures. Meteorological data can be expressed in several units. Conversion factors between various units and the standard International System of Units (S.I.) are given in Annex 1.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: an be expressed in several units. Conversion factors between various units and the standard International System of Units (S.I.) are given in Annex 1. Climatic parameters, calculated by means of the equations presented in this chapter are tabulated and displayed for different meteorological conditions in Annex 2. Only the standardized relationships are presented in this chapter. Annex 3 proposes procedures for completing data series and for statistical analysis of weather data. 3.1 METEOROLOGICAL FACTORS DETERMINING ET The meteorological factors determining evapotranspiration are those weather parameters that provide energy for vaporization and that remove water vapour from the evaporating surface. The principal weather parameters to consider are presented below. 3.1.1 Solar radiation Evapotranspiration involves the transformation of liquid water into vapour.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: weather parameters to consider are presented below. 3.1.1 Solar radiation Evapotranspiration involves the transformation of liquid water into vapour. That process requires large amounts of energy. As a result, the rate of the evapotranspiration process is determined by the amount of energy available to vaporize water. Solar radiation is the largest energy source and is able to change large quantities of liquid water into water vapour. The potential amount of radiation that can reach the evaporating surface is determined by the location and time of the year. Due to differences in the position of the sun, the potential radiation differs at various latitudes, time of day, and during different seasons. The actual solar radiation reaching the evaporating surface depends on the turbidity of the atmosphere and the presence of clouds that may reflect and absorb major parts of the radiation.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: he evaporating surface depends on the turbidity of the atmosphere and the presence of clouds that may reflect and absorb major parts of the radiation. When assessing the effect of solar radiation on evapotranspiration, one should bear in mind that not all available energy is used to vaporize water. Part of the solar energy is used to add warmth to the atmosphere and to the soil profile. 3.1.2 Air temperature The solar radiation absorbed by the atmosphere and the heat emitted by the surface increase the air temperature. The sensible heat of the surrounding air can transfer energy to the crop, if the air is warmer than the surface, and exerts as such a controlling influence on the rate of evapotranspiration. In sunny, warm weather, the loss of water by evapotranspiration is greater than in cloudy and cool weather. Chapter 3

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: 64 Crop evapotranspiration 3.1.3 Air humidity While the energy supply from the sun and the surrounding air is the main driving force for the vaporization of water, the difference between the water vapour pressure at the evapotranspiring surface and the surrounding air is the determining factor for the vapour removal. Well-watered fields in hot, dry arid regions consume large amounts of water due to the abundance of energy and the desiccating power of the dry atmosphere. In humid tropical regions, notwithstanding the high energy input, the high humidity of the air will reduce the evapotranspiration demand. In such an environment, the air may already be close to saturation, so that less additional water can be stored in the air and hence the evapotranspiration rate is lower than in arid regions.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: dy be close to saturation, so that less additional water can be stored in the air and hence the evapotranspiration rate is lower than in arid regions. 3.1.4 Wind speed The process of vapour removal depends to a large extent on wind and air turbulence which transfers large quantities of air over the evaporating surface. When vaporizing water, the air above the evaporating surface becomes gradually more saturated with water vapour. If this air is not continuously replaced with drier air by turbulence and air movement, the driving force for water vapour removal and the evapotranspiration rate decrease. The combined effect of climatic factors affecting evapotranspiration is illustrated in Figure 3.1 for two different climatic conditions.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ate decrease. The combined effect of climatic factors affecting evapotranspiration is illustrated in Figure 3.1 for two different climatic conditions. FIGURE 3.1 Illustration of the effect of wind speed on evapotranspiration in hot-dry and humidwarm weather conditions wind speed (m/s) 0 0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0 2.5 3.0 reference evapotranspiration hot and dry humid and warm Source: FAO56, 1998 The evapotranspiration demand is high in hot dry weather due to the dryness of the air and generally large amounts of energy available as direct solar radiation and sensible heat. Under these circumstances, much water vapour can be stored in the air while wind may promote the transport of water allowing more water vapour to be taken up. On the other hand, under humid weather conditions, the high humidity of the air and the presence of clouds cause the evapotranspiration rate to be lower. The effect on

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: 65 3. Meteorological variables and parameters evapotranspiration of increasing wind speeds for the two different climatic conditions is illustrated by the slope of the curves in Figure 3.1. The drier the atmosphere, the larger the effect of wind speed on ET and the greater the slope of the curve. For humid conditions, the wind can only replace saturated air at the plant surface with slightly less saturated air and remove heat energy. Consequently, the wind speed affects the evapotranspiration rate to a lesser extent than under arid conditions where small variations in wind speed may result in larger variations in the evapotranspiration rate. 3.2 ATMOSPHERIC PARAMETERS Several relationships are available to express climatic parameters. The effect of the principal weather parameters on evapotranspiration can be assessed with the help of these equations.

In traditional and modern automatic weather stations the air temperature is measured inside shelters (Stevenson screens, or ventilated, or naturally aspirated radiation shields) placed in accordance with World Meteorological Organization (WMO) standards at 2 m above the ground. The shelters are designed to protect the instruments from direct exposure to solar heating. The louvered construction promotes free air movement around the instruments. Air temperature is measured with thermometers, thermistors or thermocouples mounted in the shelter. Minimum and maximum thermometers record the minimum and maximum air temperature over a 24-hour period and use mercury and alcohol.

Older measurement systems have used bimetallic thermographs as mechanical temperature recorders. These were easy to read and maintain. However, mechanical thermographs require verification and adjustment of the position of the pen recorder to plot the instantaneous temperature on paper over a day or week. These instruments were usually installed in shelters that were naturally ventilated. Modern temperature sensors are generally the thermistor or the thermocouple. In agrometeorology, vapour pressure, dewpoint temperature and relative humidity are common expressions to indicate air humidity. Vapour pressure Water vapour is a gas, and its pressure contributes to the total atmospheric pressure.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: re common expressions to indicate air humidity. Vapour pressure Water vapour is a gas, and its pressure contributes to the total atmospheric pressure. The amount of water in the air is related directly to the partial pressure exerted by the water vapour in the air and is, therefore, a direct measure of the air water content. When air is enclosed above an evaporating water surface, an equilibrium is reached between the water molecules escaping and returning to the water reservoir. At that moment, the air is said to be saturated since it cannot store any extra water molecules. The corresponding pressure is called the saturation vapour pressure (e o(T)). The number of water molecules that can be stored in the air depends on the temperature (T). The higher the air temperature, the higher the storage capacity, and the higher its saturation vapour pressure (Figure 3.2).

At low temperatures, the slope is small and varies only slightly as the temperature rises. At high temperatures, the slope is large and small changes in T result in large changes in slope. The slope of the saturation vapour pressure curve, ∆, is an important parameter in describing vaporization and is required in the equations for calculating ETo from climatic data. The actual vapour pressure (e a) is the vapour pressure exerted by the actual quantity of water in the air.

When the air is not saturated, the actual vapour pressure will be lower than the saturation vapour pressure. The difference between the saturation and actual vapour pressure is called the vapour pressure deficit or saturation deficit and is an accurate indicator of the actual evaporative capacity of the air. In standard S.I. units, pressure is no longer expressed in centimetre of water, millimetre of mercury, bars, atmosphere, etc., but in pascals (Pa). text: 69 3. Meteorological variables and parameters Relative humidity is the ratio between the amount of water the ambient air actually holds and the amount it could hold at the same temperature. It is dimensionless and is commonly given as a percentage. Although the actual vapour pressure might be relatively constant throughout the day, the relative humidity fluctuates between a maximum near sunrise and a minimum around early afternoon (Figure 3.3). The variation of the relative humidity is the result of the fact that the saturation vapour pressure is determined by the air temperature. As the temperature changes during the day, the relative humidity also changes substantially.

The vapour pressure is commonly derived from relative humidity or dewpoint temperature. Relative humidity is measured directly with hygrometers. Older mechanical systems in mechanicallybased field stations used hair hygrometers where the hair changes its length in response to changes in air humidity. These systems were normally operated as mechanical hygrographs.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: hygrometers where the hair changes its length in response to changes in air humidity. These systems were normally operated as mechanical hygrographs. Measurements with hair hygrometers tend to lose accuracy with dust and aging of the hair. Modern electronic hygrometers use films from a dielectric polymer that changes its dielectric constant with changes in surface moisture, thus inducing a variation in the capacity of a condensator using that dielectric. These instruments are normally called dielectric polymer capacitive hygrometers. Accuracy can be higher than for hair hygrometers, the systems can be fully automated, and modern electronic sensors require little maintenance. Vapour pressure can be measured indirectly with psychrometers that measure the temperature difference between two thermometers, the so-called dry and wet bulb thermometers.

The dry bulb thermometer measures the temperature of the air. The bulb of the wet bulb thermometer is covered with a wick that is kept constantly saturated with distilled water. Evaporation of water from the wick, requiring energy, lowers the temperature of the thermometer. The drier the air, the larger the evaporative cooling and the larger the temperature drop. Usually, the dry and wet bulb thermometers are swung in the air by hand to produce sufficient air flow past the bulbs. The Assmann psychrometer has a forced ventilation of the wet bulb and dry bulb thermometers. When wet and dry bulb instruments are placed inside a naturally ventilated inside a shelter, problems can arise if air flow is not sufficient to maintain an appropriate evaporation rate and associated cooling. In more modern systems, the dry and wet bulb temperatures are measured by thermocouples or by thermistors, the so-called thermocouple psychrometers and thermo-sound psychrometers. These psychrometers are used in automatic weather stations and, when properly maintained and operated, tend to provide accurate measurements.

The dewpoint temperature is measured with dewpoint meters. The underlying principle of some types of apparatus is the cooling of the ambient air until dew formation occurs. The corresponding temperature is the dewpoint temperature. Measurement systems can use a mirror like metallic surface that is artificially cooled until vapour condenses on it and blocks the reading of reflected light. Other dew sensor systems use chemical or electric properties of certain materials that are altered when absorbing water vapour. Instruments for measuring dew point temperature require careful operation and maintenance and are seldom available in weather stations.

Relative humidity and dewpoint temperature data can be notoriously plagued by measurement errors. Measurement error is common for both older hygro-thermograph types of instruments and older electronic instruments prior to about the year 2000. The local intensity of radiation is, however, determined by the angle between the direction of the sun’s rays and the normal to the surface of the atmosphere. This angle will change during the day and will be different at different latitudes and during different seasons.

The solar radiation received at the top of the earth’s atmosphere on a horizontal surface is called the extraterrestrial (solar) or exo-atmospheric radiation, R a. If the sun is directly overhead, the angle of incidence is zero and the extraterrestrial radiation is 0.0820 MJ m-2 min-1. As seasons change, the position of the sun, the length of the day and, hence, R a change as well. Extraterrestrial radiation is thus a function of latitude, date and time of day. text: 77 3. Meteorological variables and parameters Solar or shortwave radiation (Rs) As the radiation penetrates the atmosphere, some of the radiation is scattered, reflected or absorbed by the atmospheric gases, clouds and dust. The amount of radiation reaching a horizontal plane is known as the solar radiation, R s. Because the sun emits energy by means of electromagnetic waves characterized by short wavelengths, solar radiation is also referred to as shortwave radiation. For a cloudless day, R s is roughly 75 percent of extra-terrestrial radiation due to about 25 percent of R a absorbed or scattered in the atmosphere. On a cloudy day, additional radiation is scattered or absorbed by clouds, but even with extremely dense cloud cover, about 25 percent of the extraterrestrial radiation may still reach the earth’s surface mainly as diffuse sky radiation.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: h extremely dense cloud cover, about 25 percent of the extraterrestrial radiation may still reach the earth’s surface mainly as diffuse sky radiation. Solar radiation is also known as global radiation, meaning that it is the sum of direct shortwave radiation from the sun and diffuse sky radiation from all upward angles. Relative shortwave radiation (Rs/Rso) The relative shortwave radiation is the ratio of the solar radiation (R s) to the clear-sky solar radiation (Rso). Rs is the solar radiation that actually reaches the earth’s surface in a given period, while Rso is the solar radiation that would reach the same surface during the same period but under cloudless conditions. The relative shortwave radiation is a way to express the cloudiness of the atmosphere; the cloudier the sky the smaller the ratio. The ratio varies between about 0.33 (dense cloud cover) and 1 (clear sky).

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: e cloudiness of the atmosphere; the cloudier the sky the smaller the ratio. The ratio varies between about 0.33 (dense cloud cover) and 1 (clear sky). In the absence of a direct measurement of Rn, the relative shortwave radiation is used in the computation of the net longwave radiation. Relative sunshine duration (n/N) The relative sunshine duration is another ratio that expresses the cloudiness of the atmosphere. It is the ratio of the actual duration of sunshine, n, to the maximum possible duration of sunshine or daylight hours N. In the absence of any clouds, the actual duration of sunshine is equal to the daylight hours (n = N) and the ratio is one, while on completely cloudy days n and, consequently, the ratio may be zero. In the absence of a direct measurement of Rs, the relative sunshine duration, n/N, can be used to derive solar radiation from extraterrestrial radiation.

text: 78 Crop evapotranspiration Albedo (α) and net solar radiation (R ns) A considerable amount of solar radiation reaching the earth’s surface is reflected. The fraction, a, of the solar radiation reflected by the surface is known as the albedo. The albedo is highly variable for different surfaces and for the angle of incidence or slope of the ground surface. It may be as large as 0.95 for freshly fallen snow and as small as 0.05 for wet bare soil or open water. A green vegetation cover has an albedo of about 0.20-0.25. For the green grass reference crop, a is assumed to have a value of 0.23. The net solar radiation, Rns, is the fraction of the solar radiation Rs that is not reflected from the surface. Its value is (1 − a)R s. Net longwave radiation (Rnl) The solar radiation absorbed by the earth is converted to heat energy.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: flected from the surface. Its value is (1 − a)R s. Net longwave radiation (Rnl) The solar radiation absorbed by the earth is converted to heat energy. By several processes, including the emission of radiation, the earth loses this energy. The earth, which is at a much lower temperature than the sun, emits radiative energy with wavelengths longer than those from the sun. Therefore, the terrestrial radiation is referred to as longwave radiation. The emitted longwave radiation (R l, up) is absorbed by the atmosphere or is lost into space. As a consequence of the atmosphere being above absolute zero K, the atmosphere radiates energy of its own, as illustrated in Figure 3.6. Part of the radiation finds its way back to the earth’s surface. The longwave radiation received at the surface from the atmosphere (R l, down) helps to sustain surface temperature.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: way back to the earth’s surface. The longwave radiation received at the surface from the atmosphere (R l, down) helps to sustain surface temperature. Consequently, the earth’s surface both emits and receives longwave radiation. The difference between outgoing and incoming longwave radiation is called the net longwave radiation, R nl. As the outgoing longwave radiation is almost always greater than the incoming longwave radiation, a positive Rnl represents an energy loss from the surface. Net radiation (Rn) The net radiation, R n, is the difference between incoming and outgoing radiation of both short and long wavelengths. It is the balance between the energy absorbed, reflected, and emitted by the earth’s surface or the difference between the incoming net shortwave (R ns) and the net outgoing longwave (R nl) radiation (Figure 3.6).

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: mitted by the earth’s surface or the difference between the incoming net shortwave (R ns) and the net outgoing longwave (R nl) radiation (Figure 3.6). R n is normally positive during the daytime and negative during the nighttime. The total daily value for Rn is almost always positive over a period of 24 hours, except in extreme conditions at high latitudes. text: 79 3. Meteorological variables and parameters Soil heat flux (G) In making estimates of evapotranspiration, all terms of the energy balance (Equation 1.1) should be considered. The soil heat flux, G, is the energy that is utilized in heating the soil. G is positive when the soil is warming and negative when the soil is cooling. Although the soil heat flux is small compared to R n and may often be ignored, the amount of energy gained or lost by the soil in this process should theoretically be subtracted or added to Rn when estimating evapotranspiration. 3.3.2 Units The standard unit used in this guideline to express energy received on a unit surface per unit time is megajoules per square meter per day (MJ m -2 day-1) or megajoules per square meter per hour (MJ m -2 hr -1). For hourly or shorter time periods, radiation is expressed in (MJ m -2 hr -1) for use in the FAO-PM ET o equation.

It may also be expressed as watts per square meter (W m -2). In some meteorological bulletins, other units might be used, or radiation might even be expressed in units no longer accepted as standard S.I. units, such as calories cm -2 day-1. The instruments contain a sensor installed on a horizontal surface that measures the intensity of the total solar radiation, i.e. both direct and diffuse radiation from clear sky and/or cloudy conditions. Solar radiation is most commonly measured with pyranometers. Pyranometers measure the shortwave incoming radiation over a solid angle in the shape of a hemisphere oriented upwards.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ly measured with pyranometers. Pyranometers measure the shortwave incoming radiation over a solid angle in the shape of a hemisphere oriented upwards. In the most common “glassed dome” pyranometers, a thermopile is used within the instrument as the sensor, where thermal gradients are measured across hot and cold areas (black and white) or as conducted into the instrument base (solid black). The radiation intensity is proportional to the temperature differences between the sensing areas. Accuracy depends upon the sensitivity and age of the material used in the sensors, the response time and the distortion characteristics of the material constituting the dome covering the sensors. A second type of pyranometer that is less expensive and that is gaining acceptance is the silicon diode instrument where electric current is generated by a photo sensitive diode in proportion to solar intensity.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: is gaining acceptance is the silicon diode instrument where electric current is generated by a photo sensitive diode in proportion to solar intensity. Ordinarily, silicon diode pyranometers are not fully sensitive to the full spectrum of visible light, and the calibration of the instrument is only valid for upward-facing solar measurements. When a pyranometer is oriented downwards it measures the reflected shortwave radiation, and is thus called an albedometer. When two pyranometers are associated they must have full sensitivity to all spectra of visible light. This is important since together, with one oriented upwards and the other downwards, the net short-wave radiation can be measured by subtracting one reading from the other. The instrument is then called a net pyranometer.

A point of caution is that any instrument used as an albedometer or net pyranometer composition of reflected light from vegetation is biased toward green. Therefore, most albedometers must be of the glass domed thermopile type and not the photo diode type. Where pyranometers are not available, solar radiation can be estimated from the duration of bright sunshine. Sunshine duration, n, is most commonly recorded with the CampbellStokes heliograph. This instrument records periods of bright sunshine by using a glass globe that acts as a lens. The sun rays are concentrated at a focal point that burns a hole in a specially treated card mounted concentrically with the sphere.
