Net longwave and net shortwave radiation can be measured by recording the difference in output between sensors facing upward and downward, with both covering a solid angle in the shape of a hemisphere. In a net radiometer where a single output of R n is produced, the glass domes are replaced by polyethylene domes that have a transmission range for both shortwave and longwave radiation. The sensors for net radiation are made from several thermocouples sensing heat generated by radiation from all wavelengths. All radiometers transform the radiation energy into thermal energy, a portion of which is transformed into an electric voltage gradient that provides appropriate conditions for continuous recording using dataloggers.

Four component radiometers measure incoming shortwave, reflected shortwave, incoming longwave and emitted longwave radiation all separately. Four component radiometers are generally considered to be more accurate than integrated net radiometers. They have the advantage that their four component measurements can each be quality assured separately. In addition, upward and downward facing components can be swapped periodically, for a few moments, by inverting the instrument. This provides a verification that both shortwave sensors have similar readings and that both longwave sensors have similar readings.

A more accurate estimate for Rso is obtained by considering the sun’s angle through the atmosphere and the amount of water vapor, which is variable from day to day and is an effective absorber of solar radiation.

Net longwave radiation (Rnl) The net longwave radiation is defined as the difference between longwave radiation emitted and reflected from the surface and the longwave radiation emitted to the surface from the atmosphere. The rate of longwave energy emission is proportional to the absolute temperature of the surface raised to the fourth power. This relation is expressed quantitatively by the Stefan-Boltzmann law. The net energy flux is less than that emitted from the earth’s surface due to the absorption and downward radiation from the sky. Water vapour, clouds, carbon dioxide and dust are absorbers and emitters of longwave radiation. Their concentrations should be known when assessing the net outgoing flux.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: , carbon dioxide and dust are absorbers and emitters of longwave radiation. Their concentrations should be known when assessing the net outgoing flux. In general, the longwave radiation emitted from the surface is greater than the longwave radiation emitted to the surface from the sky. This is because, under sunlit conditions, the surface tends to be warmer than the effective atmospheric temperature. As humidity and cloudiness play an important role, the Stefan-Boltzmann law is corrected by these two factors when estimating the net outgoing flux of longwave radiation.

Wind direction refers to the direction from which the wind is blowing. For the computation of evapotranspiration, wind speed is the relevant variable. As wind speed at a given location varies with time, it is necessary to express it as an average over a given time interval. Wind speed is given in meters per second (m s -1) or kilometres per day (km day -1).

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: necessary to express it as an average over a given time interval. Wind speed is given in meters per second (m s -1) or kilometres per day (km day -1). For the standardized calculation of evapotranspiration with the PM equation, wind speed measured at 2 m or transformed to an equivalent wind speed at 2 m above the surface is required. Wind speed is measured with anemometers. The anemometers commonly used in weather stations are composed of cups or propellers that are turned by the force of the wind. By counting the number of revolutions over a given time period, the average

text: 94 Crop evapotranspiration wind speed over the measuring period is computed. In some modern weather stations, sonic anemometers are used. These have the advantage of having no moving parts or bearings that require maintenance. Measurements by cup and propeller anemometers are reliable provided that maintenance ensures appropriate functioning of the mechanical parts. Older designs of anemometers utilize mechanical counters as the output device. Modern anemometers may be equipped with generators giving a voltage signal that is proportional to the wind speed. Other anemometers may be equipped with small magnetic reed switches or with optoelectronic couplers that generate electric impulses in proportion to the wind speed. The electronic devices are utilized in automatic weather stations.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: lectronic couplers that generate electric impulses in proportion to the wind speed. The electronic devices are utilized in automatic weather stations. Anemometers that collect wind speed data to be used to calculate ETo are always placed at a height not less than 2 m above the ground, following recommendations by WMO. The accuracy of wind speed measurements depends on the upwind fetch as much as on instrumentation. A large upwind fetch that is free of buildings and trees is definitely required for representative measurements. In many agrometeorological weather stations, it may be preferred to place the anemometer at 3 to 4 m above the ground surface so that the anemometer has less opportunity to be obstructed or influenced by tall crops, such as maize, growing in the vicinity. The wind speed measurement is then adjusted, numerically, to an equivalent wind speed at 2 m (Equation 3.50).

Therefore, wind speed is slowest at the surface and increases with height. For this reason, anemometers are placed at a chosen standard height, i.e. 10 m in meteorology and 2, 3 or 4 m in agrometeorology. Agrometeorological stations are intended to be sited in cropped areas where instruments are exposed to atmospheric conditions similar to those for the surrounding crops. In these stations, air temperature and humidity, wind speed and solar radiation or sunshine duration are typically measured at 2 m above an extensive surface of grass or short crop. Where needed and feasible, the cover of the station is irrigated. Guidelines for the establishment and maintenance of agrometeorological stations are given in the FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 27. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has published, since 1950, the Guide to Instruments and Methods of Observation (WMONo. 8).

text: 96 Crop evapotranspiration Data collected at stations other than agrometeorological stations require a careful analysis of their validity before their use. For example, in aeronautic stations, data relevant to aviation are measured. As airports are often situated near urban conditions and away from irrigated areas, temperatures are often higher than those found in rural agricultural areas as explained in Chapter 2. Wind speed is commonly measured at 10 m height above the ground surface and needs to be adjusted to the standard 2 m height for the ETo estimate (Figure 3.7). The country’s national meteorological services should be contacted for information on the climatic data collected at various types of weather stations in the country. National services commonly publish meteorological bulletins listing processed climatic data from the various stations.

text: eather stations in the country. National services commonly publish meteorological bulletins listing processed climatic data from the various stations. As described in Chapter 2, gridded weather data sets are becoming commonly available. It is essential that those data be assessed for quality and representativeness for use in estimating ETo. 3.6 ESTIMATING MISSING CLIMATIC DATA The assessment of the reference evapotranspiration with the FAO-PM ET o method is developed in Chapter 4. The calculation of ET o with the FAO-PM ET o equation requires hourly, daily, ten-day, or monthly maximum and minimum air temperature (Tmax and T min), actual vapour pressure (e a), net radiation (R n calculated from R s) and wind speed standardized to 2 m (u 2).

text: imum air temperature (Tmax and T min), actual vapour pressure (e a), net radiation (R n calculated from R s) and wind speed standardized to 2 m (u 2). If some of the required weather data are missing or cannot be calculated, it is strongly recommended that the user estimate the missing climatic data with one of the following procedures and continue to use the FAO-PM ET o equation. The use of an alternative ETo calculation procedure, requiring only limited meteorological parameters, is less recommended. Procedures to estimate missing humidity, solar radiation and wind speed data are given in this section. 3.6.1 Estimating missing humidity data Where humidity data are lacking or are of questionable quality, an estimate of actual vapour pressure, ea, can be obtained by assuming that the dewpoint temperature (Tdew) is near the daily minimum temperature (T min).

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: stimate of actual vapour pressure, ea, can be obtained by assuming that the dewpoint temperature (Tdew) is near the daily minimum temperature (T min). This statement implicitly assumes that at sunrise, when the air temperature is close to T min, that the near-surface air over a well-watered, transpiring surface is nearly saturated with water vapour and the relative humidity is nearly 100 percent. Reasons for this are described in Chapter 2 and procedures to estimate Tdew are presented in Chapter 2. 3.6.2 Estimating missing radiation data Net radiation measuring devices, requiring professional control, have rarely been installed in agrometeorological stations. In the absence of direct measurement, longwave and net radiation can be derived from more commonly observed weather parameters, i.e., solar radiation or sunshine hours, air temperature and vapour pressure.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: radiation can be derived from more commonly observed weather parameters, i.e., solar radiation or sunshine hours, air temperature and vapour pressure. Where solar radiation is not measured, it can be estimated from measured hours of bright sunshine. However, where daily sunshine hours (n) are not available, solar radiation data cannot be computed with the calculation procedures previously presented. This section presents additional alternative methods to estimate solar radiation data. Solar radiation data from a nearby weather station This method relies on the fact that for the same month and often for the same day, the variables affecting incoming solar radiation, R s, and sunshine duration, n, are similar throughout a given region. This implies or requires that: (i) the size of the region is small; (ii) the air masses governing rainfall and cloudiness are nearly identical within

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: 97 3. Meteorological variables and parameters parts of the region; and (iii) the physiography of the region is almost homogenous. Differences in relief should be negligible as they strongly influence the movement of air masses. Under such conditions, radiation data observed at nearby stations can be used. Caution should be used when applying this method to mountainous and coastal areas where differences in exposure and altitude could be important or where cloudiness and rainfall are variable due to convective conditions. Moreover, data from a station located nearby but situated on the other side of a mountain may not be transferable as conditions governing cloud formation and radiation may be different. The user should observe climatic conditions in both locations and obtain information from local persons concerning general differences in cloud cover and type.

Where the north-south distance to a weather station within the same homogeneous region exceeds 50 km so that the value for R a changes, the R s measurement should be adjusted using the ratio of the solar to extraterrestrial radiation, R s/Ra: Rs,reg RS = −−−− −− Ra (3.51)Ra,reg where R s,reg solar radiation at the regional location [MJ m -2 day-1], R a,reg extraterrestrial radiation at the regional location [MJ m -2 day-1]. Once the solar radiation has been derived from the radiation data of a nearby station, the net longwave radiation (Equation 3.42) and the net radiation (Equation 3.43) can be calculated. If using the method for daily estimates of ET o, a more careful analysis of weather data in the importing and exporting meteorological stations has to be performed to verify whether both stations are in the same homogeneous climatic region and are close enough to experience similar conditions within the same day. The analysis should include the comparison of daily weather data from both stations, particularly the maximum and minimum air temperature and humidity. In fact, similar cloudiness and sunshine durations are related to similarities in temperature and humidity trends. Related statistical procedures are described in Annex 3.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: diness and sunshine durations are related to similarities in temperature and humidity trends. Related statistical procedures are described in Annex 3. Generally, daily calculations of ET o with estimated radiation data are justified when utilized as a sum or an average over a several-day period. This is the case for the computation of the mean evapotranspiration demand between successive irrigations or when planning irrigation schedules. Under these conditions, the relative error for one day often counterbalances the error for another day of the averaging period. Daily estimates should not be utilized as true daily estimates but only in averages over the period under consideration. Solar radiation data derived from air temperature difference The difference between the maximum and minimum air temperature is related to the degree of cloud cover in a location.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: from air temperature difference The difference between the maximum and minimum air temperature is related to the degree of cloud cover in a location. Clear-sky conditions result in high temperatures during the day (Tmax), because the atmosphere is transparent to the incoming solar radiation, and in low temperatures during the night (T min), because less downward longwave radiation is emitted by the atmosphere. On the other hand, in overcast conditions, T max is relatively smaller because a significant part of the incoming solar radiation never reaches the earth’s surface and is absorbed and reflected by the clouds. Similarly, T min will be relatively higher because the cloud cover acts as a blanket and decreases the net outgoing longwave radiation.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: by the clouds. Similarly, T min will be relatively higher because the cloud cover acts as a blanket and decreases the net outgoing longwave radiation. Therefore, the difference between the maximum and minimum air temperature (Tmax − T min) can be used as an indicator of the fraction of extraterrestrial radiation that reaches the earth’s surface. This principle has been utilized by Hargreaves and Samani to develop estimates of ETo using only air temperature data.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: 98 Crop evapotranspiration The Hargreaves-Samani radiation formula, adjusted and validated at several weather stations in a variety of climate conditions, becomes: Rs = kRs √ (Tmax - Tmin) Ra (3.52) where R a extraterrestrial radiation [MJ m-2 d-1], T max maximum air temperature [°C], T min minimum air temperature [°C], k Rs empirical adjustment coefficient [°C-0.5]. The fraction of extraterrestrial radiation that reaches the earth’s surface, R s/Ra, ranges from about 0.25 on a day with dense cloud cover to about 0.75 to 0.80 on a cloudless day with a clear sky, depending on elevation. R s estimated by Equation 3.52 should be limited to ≤ Rso from Equation 3.34 or 3.35. The square root of the temperature difference is closely related to the existing daily solar radiation in a given location.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: rom Equation 3.34 or 3.35. The square root of the temperature difference is closely related to the existing daily solar radiation in a given location. The adjustment coefficient k Rs was originally recommended by Hargreaves and Samani as 0.16 for land locations, not influenced by large water bodies, and 0.19 for “coastal” locations. However, k Rs is empirical and relates to the atmospheric conditions that influence the availability of incoming solar radiation at crop and natural surfaces, and so with the availability of energy for evaporation. Thus, k Rs has been shown to vary spatially with site elevation and the distance to large water bodies. In addition, its value may increase with the aridity of the site and with wind speed.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ally with site elevation and the distance to large water bodies. In addition, its value may increase with the aridity of the site and with wind speed. A useful approach is to estimate k Rs values using various long-term (ideally > 30-years) average weather variables that allow for characterizing the site location: the difference between the maximum and minimum air temperature (TD = Tmax −Tmin), RH and u2. In practice, the site averages are computed from available local observations or from a nearby weather station, where climates should be similar, when such data are not available locally (Example 3.14).

When averaged over longer periods, error in estimates and occurrence of outlying values should decrease. 3.6.3 Missing wind speed data Wind speed data from a nearby weather station Importing wind speed data from a nearby station, as for radiation data, relies on the fact that the air flow above a “homogeneous” region may have relatively large variations through the course of a day but small variations when referring to longer periods or the total for the day. Data from a nearby station may be imported where air masses are of the same origin or where the same fronts govern air flows in the region and where the relief is similar. When importing wind speed data from another station, the regional climate, trends in the variation of other meteorological parameters and relief should be comparable.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ind speed data from another station, the regional climate, trends in the variation of other meteorological parameters and relief should be comparable. Strong winds are often associated with low relative humidity and light winds are common with high relative humidity. Thus, trends in variation of daily maximum and minimum relative humidities should be similar in both locations. In mountainous areas, data should not necessarily be imported from the nearest station but from nearby stations with similar elevation and exposure to the dominant winds. The paired stations may even vary from one season to another, depending on the dominant winds. Imported wind speed data can be used when making monthly estimates of evapotranspiration. Daily calculations are justified when utilized as a sum or average over a several-day period, such as a week or decade.

Empirical estimates of monthly wind speed As the variation in wind speed averaged over monthly periods is relatively small and fluctuates around average values, monthly values of wind speed may be estimated. The “average” wind speed estimates may be selected from information available for the regional climate but should take seasonal changes into account. General values are suggested in Table 3.2. The results are different at locations characterized by light-moderate wind speeds with an overestimation tendency when the default u2 value is used in ETo estimation. In general, wind speed at 2 m, u 2, should be limited to about u 2 ≥ 0.5 m s -1 when used in the FAO-PM-ETo equation. This is necessary to account for the effects of boundary layer instability and buoyancy of air in promoting exchange of vapour at the surface when air is calm. This effect occurs when the wind speed is small, and buoyancy of warm air induces air exchange at the surface; u2 ≥ 0.5 m s-1 in the ETo equation improves the estimation accuracy.

text: 106 Crop evapotranspiration 3.6.4 Minimum data requirements: the Penman-Monteith temperature approach (PMT) The PMT approach applies the FAO standardized Penman-Monteith equation where solar radiation, vapour pressure and wind data may be estimated when missing or when found to be faulty or nonrepresentative. Many of the suggested procedures rely upon maximum and minimum air temperature measurements. Unfortunately, there is no dependable way to estimate air temperature when it is missing. Therefore, it is suggested that maximum and minimum daily air temperature data are the minimum data requirements necessary to apply the FAO-PM equation. Figure 3.12 presents an example of the successful application of PMT, when using Equation 3.52 for estimating R s and Equations 3.53 and 3.54a for estimating k Rs and using the default u 2 value of 2 m/s.

Meteorological variables and parameters As recommended in the section above, the FAO Penman-Monteith Temperature method, PMT, is recommended over other empirical ET o methods, even when daily maximum and minimum air temperature data are the only data available. This is because the PM equation contains appropriate and physically based relationships among weather variables and because the missing weather variables can be relatively accurately estimated using informed procedures described in the previous section and in Chapter 2. Therefore, the PM equation is likely to produce ET o estimates that are sensitive to the expected behaviours of the missing weather variables. This is in contrast to a stand-alone temperature-based method such as the Hargreaves-Samani method that has no means to change its behaviour under different general weather conditions such as high wind locations vs.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)

With this in mind, however, the Hargreaves-Samani ET o equation is provided in the following section as a backup procedure. 3.6.5 An alternative equation for computing ET o when key weather data are missing: the Hargreaves-Samani equation When solar radiation data, relative humidity data and/or wind speed data are missing, they should be estimated using the procedures presented in the previous section.

text: 113 4. Determination of ETo Determination of ETo This chapter demonstrates how crop reference evapotranspiration (ET o) is determined either from meteorological data or from pan evaporation. The FAO Penman-Monteith method is maintained as the sole standard method for the computation of ET o from meteorological data. The method itself is introduced in Chapter 2, and the computation of all data required for the calculation of ET o is described and discussed in Chapter 3. This chapter presents guidelines to calculate ETo with different time steps, ranging from hours to months, and with missing climatic data. The ETo calculation can be done by hand with the help of a calculation sheet, or by means of a computer. The use of computers is highly recommended. ETo can also be approximated from the evaporation loss from a water surface.

text: 114 Crop evapotranspiration 4.1.1 Calculation procedure Calculation sheet ETo can be estimated for daily (24-hour) calculation time steps by means of the calculation sheet presented in Box 4.1. The calculation sheet refers to tables in Annex 2 for the determination of some of the climatic parameters. The calculation procedure consists of the following steps: 1. Derivation of some climatic parameters from the daily maximum (T max) and minimum (Tmin) air temperature, altitude (z) and mean wind speed (u 2). 2. Calculation of the vapour pressure deficit (e s − ea). The saturation vapour pressure (es) is derived from T max and T min, while the actual vapour pressure (e a) can be derived from the dewpoint temperature (T dew), from maximum (RH max) and minimum (RHmin) relative humidity, or from the maximum (RHmax), or from mean relative humidity (RHmean). 3.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: erature (T dew), from maximum (RH max) and minimum (RHmin) relative humidity, or from the maximum (RHmax), or from mean relative humidity (RHmean). 3. Determination of the net radiation (Rn) as the difference between the net shortwave radiation (Rns) and the net longwave radiation (R nl). In the calculation sheet, the effect of soil heat flux (G) is ignored for daily calculations as the magnitude of the flux in this case is relatively small. The net radiation, expressed in MJ m -2 day-1, is converted to mm day -1 (equivalent evaporation) in the FAO-PM ET o equation by using 0.408 as the conversion factor within the equation. 4. ETo is obtained by combining the results of the previous steps. Examples 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3 present typical cases using the calculation sheet for monthly, daily, and hourly calculation timesteps.

Determination of ETo Ten-day or monthly time step Notwithstanding the non-linearity in the FAO-PM ET o equation and some weather parameter methods, mean ten-day or monthly weather data can be used to compute the mean ten-day or monthly values for the reference evapotranspiration. The value of the reference evapotranspiration calculated with mean monthly weather data is indeed very similar to the average of the daily ETo values calculated with daily average weather data for that month. The meteorological data consist of: • Air temperature: ten-day or monthly average daily maximum (T max) and average daily minimum temperature (Tmin). • Air humidity: ten-day or monthly average of the daily actual vapour pressure (e a) derived from psychrometric, dewpoint or relative humidity data. • Wind speed: ten-day or monthly average of daily wind speed data transformed to a 2 m height (u2).

The extraterrestrial radiation (Ra) and daylight hours (N) for a specific day of the month can be computed using Equations 3.18 and 3.31 in Chapter 3, or can be selected from Tables A2.5 and A2.6 in Annex 2. When the soil is warming (spring) or cooling (autumn), the soil heat flux (G) for monthly periods may become significant relative to the mean monthly R n. In these cases G cannot be ignored and its value should be determined from the mean monthly air temperatures of the previous and next month.

text: 121 4. Determination of ETo Hourly time step In areas where substantial changes in wind speed, dewpoint or cloudiness occur during the day, calculation of the ETo equation using hourly time steps is generally better than using 24-hour calculation time steps. Such weather changes can cause 24-hour means to misrepresent the evaporative power of the environment during parts of the day and may introduce errors in the calculations. However, under most conditions, the application of the FAO-PM ETo equation with 24-hour data produces accurate results. With the advent of electronic, automated weather stations, weather data are increasingly reported for hourly or shorter periods. Therefore, in situations where calculations are computerized, the FAO-PM ETo equation can be applied on an hourly basis with good results.

AI is highly effective in analyzing time series data. These attributes make these processes potentially valuable for efficiently forecasting and understanding complex time-dependent phenomena. However, precautions must be made prior to and during their application, especially in ET data assessment and extension.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: 127 4. Determination of ETo The performance of AI models relies heavily on the quality and availability of data. AI can not readily correct for faulty data that may be ingested into the AI process, but are not recognized as faulty. Nor does AI provide a replacement for physics-based relationships. These guidelines wish to be quite clear that the FAO-PM equation does NOT need to be replaced by an AI-generated simpler equation, even when some weather data are missing. The FAO-PM equation is a physics-based equation that contains the internal, physical responses and sensitivities to impacts of the four primary weather parameters that drive the ET process. These parameters are solar radiation (and therefore net radiation), air temperature, air humidity and wind speed.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: arameters that drive the ET process. These parameters are solar radiation (and therefore net radiation), air temperature, air humidity and wind speed. These parameters have strong interactions within the ET process that utilizes knowledge of available environmental energy and aerodynamic transfer processes to estimate the total transfer and transformation of energy into the vapourization of liquid water. Many practitioners are learning to use AI, but they may not be learning or adhering to the physics that govern ET processes. In addition, users of AI may not first gain or exercise an ability to recognize or to question faulty data prior to ingestion into an AI procedure.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: s. In addition, users of AI may not first gain or exercise an ability to recognize or to question faulty data prior to ingestion into an AI procedure. As a result, they may create abstract and incorrect relationships between ETo and weather data or between ET o and ground-measurements of reference ET that may not have the appropriate structures, accuracies and sensitivities. Good quality assessment and quality control (QAQC) is fundamental to the process. The QAQC step requires overview, correction and concurrence by a knowledgeable human. These guidelines make it clear that it is best to remain with the use of a physics-based reference equation, the FAO-Penman-Monteith equation, and make best estimates for missing weather data, rather than to employ an AI engine that may not adhere to all physical laws that govern ET.

The result of the latter process can be the production of tangential errors that violate physical principles. Precaution, coupled with human oversight and review, is critical. A well-designed and trained AI process may be useful for recognizing deviation of weather data from that occurring under reference (well-watered) conditions due to aridity in or surrounding a weather station. The process can then make necessary adjustments to the data using procedures similar to those addressed previously in Chapter 2. 4.3 PAN EVAPORATION METHOD 4.3.1 Pan evaporation The evaporation rate from pans filled with water is easily obtained.

text: dressed previously in Chapter 2. 4.3 PAN EVAPORATION METHOD 4.3.1 Pan evaporation The evaporation rate from pans filled with water is easily obtained. In the absence of rain, the amount of water evaporated during a period (mm day-1) corresponds with the decrease in water depth in that period. Pans provide a measurement of the integrated effect of radiation, wind, temperature and humidity on the evaporation from an open water surface. Although the pan responds in a similar fashion to the same climatic factors affecting crop transpiration, several factors produce significant differences in loss of water from a water surface and from a cropped surface. The reflection of solar radiation from water in the shallow pan might be different from the assumed 23 percent for the grass reference surface.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: rface. The reflection of solar radiation from water in the shallow pan might be different from the assumed 23 percent for the grass reference surface. Storage of heat within the pan can be appreciable and may cause significant evaporation during the night while most crops transpire only during the daytime. There are also differences in turbulence, temperature and humidity of the air immediately above the respective surfaces. Heat transfer through the sides of the pan occurs and affects the energy balance.

As the colour, size, and field position of the pan have a significant influence on the measured results, the pan coefficients are pan specific.

The siting of the pan and the pan environment also influence the results. This is particularly so where the pan is placed in fallow rather than cropped fields. text: 129 4. Determination of ETo BOX 4.2 Description of Class A pan The Class A Evaporation pan is circular, 120.7 cm in diameter and 25 cm deep. It is made of galvanized iron (22 gauge) or Monel metal (0.8 mm). The pan is mounted on a wooden open frame platform which is 15 cm above ground level. The soil is built up to within 5 cm of the bottom of the pan. The pan must be level. It is filled with water to 5 cm below the rim, and the water level should not be allowed to drop to more than 7.5 cm below the rim. The water should be regularly renewed, at least weekly, to eliminate extreme turbidity. The pan, if galvanized, is painted annually with aluminum paint. Screens over the pan are not a standard requirement and should preferably not be used. Pans should be protected by fences to keep animals from drinking.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: reens over the pan are not a standard requirement and should preferably not be used. Pans should be protected by fences to keep animals from drinking. The site should preferably be under grass, 20 by 20 m (at least 15 by 15), open on all sides to permit free circulation of the air. It is preferable that stations be located in the centre or on the leeward side of large cropped fields. Pan readings are taken daily in the early morning at the same time that precipitation is measured. Measurements are made in a stilling well that is situated in the pan near one edge. The stilling well is a metal cylinder of about 10 cm in diameter and some 20 cm deep with a small hole at the bottom.

text: 130 Crop evapotranspiration BOX 4.3 Description of Colorado sunken pan The Colorado sunken pan is 92 cm (3 ft) square and 46 cm (18 in) deep, made of 3 mm thick iron, placed in the ground with the rim 5 cm (2 in) above the soil level. Also, the dimensions 1 m square and 0.5 m deep are frequently used. The pan is painted with black tar paint. The water level is maintained at or slightly below ground level, i.e. 5-7.5 cm below the rim. Measurements are taken similarly to those for the Class A pan. Siting and environment requirements are also similar to those for the Class A pan. Sunken Colorado pans are sometimes preferred in crop water requirements studies, as these pans give a better direct estimation of the reference evapotranspiration than does the Class A pan. The disadvantage is that maintenance is more difficult and leaks are not visible.

Pan coefficients Depending on the type of pan and the size and state of the upwind buffer zone (fetch), pan coefficients will differ. The larger the upwind buffer zone, the more the air moving over the pan will be in equilibrium with the buffer zone. At equilibrium with a large fetch, the air contains more water vapour and less heat in Case A than in Case B (Figure 4.2). Pan coefficients for the Class A pan and for the Colorado sunken pan for different ground cover, fetch and climatic conditions are presented in Tables 4.1 and 4.2. For extensive areas of bare-fallow soils and no agricultural development, reduce Kp by 20 percent under hot, windy conditions; by 5-10 percent for moderate wind, temperature and humidity conditions.

text: 133 4. Determination of ETo Adjustments Under some conditions not accounted for in the tables, the presented K p coefficients may need some adjustment. This is the case in areas with no agricultural development, or where the pans are enclosed by tall crops. Not maintaining the standard colour of the pan or installing screens can affect the pan readings and will require some adjustment of the pan coefficient. In areas with no agricultural development and extensive areas of bare soils (large fetch, Case B), as found under desert or semi-desert conditions, the listed values for K p given for arid, windy areas may need to be reduced by up to 20 percent; for areas with moderate levels of wind, temperature and relative humidity, the listed values may need to be reduced by 5-10 percent; no or little reduction in K p is needed in humid, cool conditions.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: re and relative humidity, the listed values may need to be reduced by 5-10 percent; no or little reduction in K p is needed in humid, cool conditions. Where pans are placed in a small enclosure but surrounded by tall crops, for example 2.5 m high maize, the listed pan coefficients will need to be increased by up to 30 percent for dry windy climates, whereas only a 5-10 percent increase is required for calm, humid conditions. Painting the pans may affect the pan evaporation. The pan coefficients presented apply to galvanized pans annually painted with aluminium and to stainless steel pans. Little difference in E pan will occur where the inside and outside surfaces of the pan are painted white. An increase in E pan of up to 10 percent may occur when they are painted black. The material from which the pan is made may account for variations of only a few percent.

text: n of up to 10 percent may occur when they are painted black. The material from which the pan is made may account for variations of only a few percent. The level at which the water is maintained in the pan is important; resulting errors may be up to 15 percent when water levels in the Class A pan fall 10 cm below the accepted standard of between 5 and 7.5 cm below the rim. Screens mounted over pans will reduce Epan by up to 10 percent. In an attempt to avoid pans being used by birds for drinking, pans filled to the rim with water can be placed near the Class A pan; birds may prefer to use the fully filled pan. The evaporation pan should be placed in a large, secure, wire enclosure to prevent animals from entering and drinking. The turbidity of the water in the pan usually does not affect E pan by more than 5 percent.

The overall variation in Epan is not constant with time because of aging, deterioration and repainting. Recommendations The above considerations and adjustments indicate that the use of tables or the corresponding equations may not be sufficient to consider all local environmental factors influencing K p and that local adjustment may be required. To do so, an appropriate calibration of E pan against ET o computed with the Penman-Monteith method is recommended. It is recommended that the pan should be installed inside a short green cropped area with a size of a square of at least 15 by 15 m. The pan should not be installed in the centre but at a distance of at least 10 m from the green crop edge in the general upwind direction.

text: 137 5. Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc ) and its measurement Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc) and its measurement This chapter outlines the crop coefficient (K c) approach for calculating the crop evapotranspiration under standard conditions (ET c). The standard conditions refer to crops grown in large fields under excellent agronomic and soil water conditions. The crop evapotranspiration differs distinctly from the reference evapotranspiration (ETo) as the ground cover, canopy properties and aerodynamic resistance of the crop are different from grass. The effects of characteristics that distinguish field crops from grass are integrated into the crop coefficient. In the crop coefficient approach, crop evapotranspiration is calculated by multiplying ETo by Kc.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: from grass are integrated into the crop coefficient. In the crop coefficient approach, crop evapotranspiration is calculated by multiplying ETo by Kc. Differences in evaporation and transpiration between field crops and the reference grass surface can be integrated into a single crop coefficient (K c) or separated into two coefficients: a basal crop (K cb) and a soil evaporation coefficient (K e), i.e. K c = Kcb + K e. The approach to follow should be selected as a function of the purpose of the calculation, the accuracy required and the data available. A brief review of ET c measurement using ground and remote observations and sensors is added. 5.1 CALCULATION PROCEDURES 5.1.1 Direct calculation The evapotranspiration rate from a cropped surface can be directly measured by the mass transfer or the energy balance method.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: .1.1 Direct calculation The evapotranspiration rate from a cropped surface can be directly measured by the mass transfer or the energy balance method. It can also be derived from studies of the soil water balance determined from cropped fields or from lysimeters. Crop evapotranspiration can also be derived from meteorological and crop data by means of the FAO-PM ET o equation (Equation 2.1). By adjusting the albedo and the aerodynamic and canopy surface resistances to the growing characteristics of the specific crop, the evapotranspiration rate can be directly estimated using the Penman-Monteith combination equation (Equation 2.3). The albedo and resistances are, however, difficult to estimate accurately as they may vary continually during the growing season as climatic conditions change, as the crop develops, and with the wetness of the soil surface.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: as they may vary continually during the growing season as climatic conditions change, as the crop develops, and with the wetness of the soil surface. The canopy resistance will further be influenced by the soil water availability, and it increases strongly if the crop is subjected to water stress. As there is still a considerable lack of consolidated information on the aerodynamic and canopy resistances for the various cropped surfaces, the FAO-PM ETo equation is used in these guidelines only for estimating ETo, the evapotranspiration from a well-watered (hypothetical) grass surface having fixed crop height, albedo, and surface resistance. text: 138 Crop evapotranspiration 5.1.2 Crop coefficient approach In the crop coefficient approach the crop evapotranspiration, ET c, is calculated by multiplying the reference crop evapotranspiration, ET o, by a crop coefficient, Kc: ETc = Kc ETo (5.1) where ET c crop evapotranspiration [mm d-1], K c crop coefficient [dimensionless], ET o reference crop evapotranspiration [mm d-1]. Most of the effects of the various weather conditions are incorporated into the ETo estimate. Therefore, as ETo represents an index of climatic demand, K c varies predominately with the specific crop characteristics and only to a limited extent with climate. This enables the transfer of standard values for K c between locations and between climates. This has been a primary reason for the global acceptance and usefulness of the crop coefficient approach and the Kc standard values developed in past studies.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: been a primary reason for the global acceptance and usefulness of the crop coefficient approach and the Kc standard values developed in past studies. The reference ETo is defined and calculated using the FAO-PM ETo equation (Chapters 2 and 4). The crop coefficient, Kc, is basically the ratio of the crop ETc to the reference ETo, and it represents an integration of the effects of four primary characteristics that distinguish the crop from the reference grass. These characteristics are: • Crop height: the crop height influences the aerodynamic resistance term, ra, of the FAO-PM ETo equation and the turbulent transfer of vapour from the crop into the atmosphere. The r a term appears twice in the full form of the FAO-PM ET o equation. • Albedo (reflectance) of the crop-soil surface: the albedo is affected by the fraction of ground covered by vegetation and by the soil surface wetness.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: Albedo (reflectance) of the crop-soil surface: the albedo is affected by the fraction of ground covered by vegetation and by the soil surface wetness. The albedo of the crop-soil surface influences the net radiation of the surface, R n, which is the primary source of the energy exchange for the evaporation process. • Canopy resistance: the resistance of the crop to vapour transfer is affected by leaf area (number of stomata), leaf age and condition, and the degree of stomatal control. The canopy resistance influences the surface resistance, r s. • Evaporation from soil, especially exposed soil. The soil surface wetness and the fraction of ground covered by vegetation influence the surface resistance, rs. Following soil wetting, the vapour transfer rate from the soil is high, especially for crops having incomplete ground cover.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: e surface resistance, rs. Following soil wetting, the vapour transfer rate from the soil is high, especially for crops having incomplete ground cover. The combined surface resistance of the canopy and the soil determines the (bulk) surface resistance, r s. The surface resistance term in the Penman-Monteith combination Equation 2.3 represents the resistance to vapour flow from within plant leaves and from beneath the soil surface. The Kc in Equation 5.1 predicts ETc under standard conditions. The standard condition represents an upper envelope of crop evapotranspiration and represents conditions where no limitations are placed on crop growth or evapotranspiration due to water shortage, low crop density, or disease, weed, insect, or salinity pressures. The ET c estimated by Kc is adjusted if necessary to non-standard conditions.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: tage, low crop density, or disease, weed, insect, or salinity pressures. The ET c estimated by Kc is adjusted if necessary to non-standard conditions. The non-standard actual condition, which is assumed to represent the actual ET condition, is termed ET c act. ET c act is estimated and applied when any environmental condition or characteristic is known to have a negative impact on, or sets a limit on ET c. Factors for correcting ET c to ETc act are described in Chapter 8 (Part C).

text: 139 5. Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc ) and its measurement 5.2 FACTORS DETERMINING THE CROP COEFFICIENT The crop coefficient integrates the effect of characteristics that distinguish a typical field crop from the grass reference, where the standardized grass reference has a constant appearance and a complete ground cover. Consequently, different crops will have different K c coefficients. The changing characteristics of the crop over the growing season affect the K c coefficient. Finally, as evaporation is an integrated part of crop evapotranspiration, conditions affecting soil evaporation will also have an effect on K c. 5.2.1 Crop type Due to differences in albedo, crop height, aerodynamic properties, and leaf and stomata properties, the evapotranspiration from full-grown, well-watered crops differs from ETo.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: do, crop height, aerodynamic properties, and leaf and stomata properties, the evapotranspiration from full-grown, well-watered crops differs from ETo. The close spacings of plants and taller canopy height and roughness of many fullgrown agricultural crops cause these crops to have K c factors that are larger than 1. The Kc factor is often 5-10 percent higher than the reference (where Kc = 1.0), and even 15-20 percent greater for some tall crops such as maize, sorghum or sugar cane (Figure 5.1). Typical values for the crop coefficient for full-grown crops (K c mid) are listed in Tables 6.1 – 6.5 of Chapter 6. In most species, the stomata open as irradiance increases. In addition to the stomatal response to the environment, the position and number of the stomata and the resistance of the cuticula to vapour transfer determine the water loss from the crop.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: the environment, the position and number of the stomata and the resistance of the cuticula to vapour transfer determine the water loss from the crop. Species with stomata on only the lower side of the leaf and/or large leaf resistances will have relatively smaller K c values. This is the case for citrus and most deciduous fruit trees. Transpiration control and spacing of the trees, providing only 70 percent ground cover for mature trees, may cause the K c of those trees, if cultivated without a ground cover crop, to be smaller than 1.0 (Figure 5.1). 5.2.2 Climate The Kc values of Tables 6.1 – 6.5 of Chapter 6 are typical values expected for average Kc under a standard climatic condition, which is defined as a sub-humid climate with average daytime minimum relative humidity (RH min) ≈ 45% and having calm to moderate wind speeds averaging u2 = 2 m s-1.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: d as a sub-humid climate with average daytime minimum relative humidity (RH min) ≈ 45% and having calm to moderate wind speeds averaging u2 = 2 m s-1. Variations in wind speed alter the aerodynamic resistance of the crops and may alter their crop coefficients, especially for those crops that are substantially taller than the hypothetical grass reference. The effect of the difference in aerodynamic properties between the grass reference surface and agricultural crops is not only crop-specific but it also varies with the climatic conditions and crop height. Because aerodynamic properties are greater for many agricultural crops as compared to the grass reference, the ratio of ETc to ETo (i.e. Kc) for many crops increases as wind speed increases and as relative humidity decreases. More arid climates and conditions of greater wind speed will tend to have higher values for K c.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: d speed increases and as relative humidity decreases. More arid climates and conditions of greater wind speed will tend to have higher values for K c. More humid climates and conditions of lower wind speed will have lower values for K c. The relative impact of the climate on K c for full-grown crops is illustrated in Figure 5.2. The upper bounds represent extremely arid and windy conditions, while the lower bounds are valid under very humid and calm weather conditions. The ranges expected in Kc as climate and weather conditions change are quite small for short crops but are large for tall crops. Guidelines for the adjustment of K c to the climatic conditions as a function of crop height are given in Chapter 6.

text: 141 5. Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc ) and its measurement Under humid and calm wind conditions, K c becomes less dependent on the differences between the aerodynamic components of ET c and ET o and the K c values for “fullcover” agricultural crops do not exceed 1.0 by more than about 0.05. This is because full-cover agricultural crops and the reference crop of clipped grass both provide for nearly maximum absorption of shortwave radiation, which is the primary energy source for evaporation under humid and calm conditions. Generally, the albedos, α , are similar over a wide range of full-cover agricultural crops, including the reference crop.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: r humid and calm conditions. Generally, the albedos, α , are similar over a wide range of full-cover agricultural crops, including the reference crop. Because the vapour pressure deficit (e s − ea) is small under humid conditions, differences in ET caused by differences in aerodynamic resistance, r a, between the agricultural crop and the reference crop are also small, especially with low to moderate wind speed. Under arid conditions, the effect of differences in r a between the agricultural crop and the grass reference crop on ET c becomes more pronounced because the (e s − e a) term may be relatively large. The larger magnitudes of (e s − e a) amplify differences in the aerodynamic term in the numerator of the Penman-Monteith combination equation (Equation 2.1) for both the crop and the reference crop.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ferences in the aerodynamic term in the numerator of the Penman-Monteith combination equation (Equation 2.1) for both the crop and the reference crop. Hence, Kc will be larger under arid conditions when the agricultural crop has a leaf area and roughness height that are greater than that of the grass reference. Because the 1/r a term in the numerator of the FAO-PM ET o equation (Equation 2.4 and 2.5a, b) is multiplied by the vapour pressure deficit (es − ea), the ET from tall crops increases proportionately more relative to ET o than does ET from short crops when relative humidity is low. The K c for tall crops, such as those 2-3 m in height, can be as much as 30 percent higher in a windy, arid climate as compared with a calm, humid climate.

The increase in Kc is due to the influence of the larger aerodynamic roughness of the tall crop relative to grass on the transport of water vapour from the surface. 5.2.3 Soil evaporation Differences in soil evaporation and crop transpiration between field crops and the reference surface are integrated within the crop coefficient. The K c coefficient for fullcover crops primarily reflects differences in transpiration as the contribution of soil evaporation is relatively small. After rainfall or irrigation, the effect of evaporation is predominant when the crop is small and scarcely shades the ground. For such lowcover conditions, the Kc coefficient is determined largely by the frequency with which the soil surface is wetted.

Where the soil is wet for most of the time from irrigation or rain, the evaporation from the soil surface will be considerable and K c may exceed 1. On the other hand, where the soil surface is dry, evaporation is restricted, and K c will be small and might even drop to less than 0.20 (Figure 5.3). Differences in soil evaporation between the field crop and the reference surface can be forecast more precisely by using a dual crop coefficient. 5.2.4 Crop growth stages As the crop develops, the ground cover, crop height and leaf area change. Due to differences in evapotranspiration during the various growth stages, the Kc for a given crop will vary over the growing period.

text: 144 Crop evapotranspiration Crop development stage The crop development stage runs from 10 percent ground cover to effective full cover. Effective full cover for many crops occurs at the initiation of flowering. For row crops where rows commonly interlock leaves such as beans, sugar beets, potatoes and maize, effective cover can be defined as the time when some leaves of plants in adjacent rows begin to intermingle so that soil shading becomes nearly complete, or when plants reach nearly full size if no intermingling occurs. For some crops, especially those taller than 0.5 m, the average fraction of the ground surface covered by vegetation (f c) at the start of effective full cover is about 0.7-0.8. Fractions of sunlit and shaded soil and leaves do not change significantly with further growth of the crop beyond f c ≈ 0.7 to 0.8.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: is about 0.7-0.8. Fractions of sunlit and shaded soil and leaves do not change significantly with further growth of the crop beyond f c ≈ 0.7 to 0.8. It is understood that the crop or plant can continue to grow in both height and leaf area after the time of effective full cover. Because it is difficult to visually determine when densely sown vegetation such as winter and spring cereals and some grasses reach effective full cover, the more easily detectable stage of heading (flowering) is generally used for these types of crops. For dense grasses, effective full cover may occur at about 0.10-0.15 m in height. For thin stands of grass (dry rangeland), grass height may approach 0.3-0.5 m before effective full cover is reached. Densely planted forages such as alfalfa and clover reach effective full cover at about 0.3-0.4 m.

Another way to estimate the occurrence of effective full cover is when the leaf area index (LAI) reaches three in case of very dense low crops. LAI is defined as the average total area of leaves (one side) per unit area of ground surface. In the case of evergreen woody perennials, it is difficult to distinguish when crop development started and when it ends. Leaves are there and shade the ground through the full crop season. Differences in K c mostly result from the frequency of wettings by rain and irrigation covering the full surface. Partial cover of irrigation produces small impacts. In the case of deciduous woody perennials, full development of leaves is attained quickly and rain and irrigation impacts are minor.

During the crop development stage, the Kc value corresponds to the amounts of ground cover and plant development. Mid-season stage The mid-season stage runs from effective full cover to the start of maturity. The start of maturity is often indicated by the beginning of the aging, yellowing or senescence of leaves, initial leaf drop, or the browning of fruit to the degree that the crop evapotranspiration is reduced relative to the reference ET o. The mid-season stage is the longest stage for perennials and many annuals, but it may be relatively short for vegetable crops that are harvested fresh for their green vegetation. At the mid-season stage the K c reaches its maximum value.

text: 145 5. Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc ) and its measurement Late season stage The late season stage runs from the start of maturity to harvest or full senescence. The calculation for K c and ET c is presumed to end when the crop is harvested, dries out naturally, reaches full senescence, or experiences leaf drop. For some perennial vegetation in frost-free climates, crops may grow year-round so that the date of termination may be taken as the same as the date of planting or greenup. This is the case of evergreen woody perennials, which K c value may not change; however, for deciduous woody perennials K c decreases until leaf dropping or is kept relatively high if autumn irrigation is required to ensure physiological processes that determine next year yield.

The K c value at the end of the late season stage (K c end ) reflects crop and water management practices (Figure 5.5). The K c end value is high if the crop is frequently irrigated until harvested fresh. If the crop is allowed to senesce and to dry out in the field before harvest, the Kc end value will be small. Senescence is usually associated with less efficient stomatal conductance of leaf surfaces due to the effects of aging, thereby causing a reduction in Kc. 5.3 CROP EVAPOTRANSPIRATION (ETc) Crop evapotranspiration is calculated by multiplying ETo by Kc, a coefficient expressing the difference in evapotranspiration between the cropped and the reference grass surface.

The coefficient K c integrates differences in the soil evaporation and crop transpiration rate between the crop and the grass reference surface. As soil evaporation may fluctuate daily as a result of rainfall or irrigation, the single crop coefficient expresses only the time-averaged (multi-day) effects of crop evapotranspiration.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: 146 Crop evapotranspiration As the single K c coefficient averages soil evaporation and transpiration, the approach is used to compute ET c for weekly or longer time periods, although calculations may proceed on a daily time step. The single, time-averaged K c is used for planning studies and irrigation system design where the time-averaging effects of soil wetting are acceptable and relevant. This is the case for surface irrigation and set sprinkler systems where the time interval between successive irrigation is of several days, often ten days or more. For typical irrigation management, the time-averaged single K c is valid. Dual crop coefficient approach (Kcb + Ke) In the dual crop coefficient approach, the effects of crop transpiration and soil evaporation are determined separately.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: efficient approach (Kcb + Ke) In the dual crop coefficient approach, the effects of crop transpiration and soil evaporation are determined separately. Two coefficients are used: the basal crop coefficient (K cb) to describe plant transpiration, and the soil water evaporation coefficient (K e) to describe evaporation from the soil surface. The single K c coefficient is replaced by: Kc = Kcb + Ke (5.2) where K cb basal crop coefficient, K e soil water evaporation coefficient. The basal crop coefficient, K cb, is defined as the ratio of ET c to ET o when the soil surface layer is dry but where the average soil water content of the root zone is adequate to sustain full plant transpiration. The K cb represents the baseline standard Kc in the absence of the additional effects of soil wetting by irrigation or precipitation.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: t transpiration. The K cb represents the baseline standard Kc in the absence of the additional effects of soil wetting by irrigation or precipitation. The basal crop coefficient, K cb, can also be defined as the ratio of transpiration, T c to ETo. Therefore, it is also called the transpiration coefficient. The soil evaporation coefficient, Ke, describes the evaporation component from the soil surface. If the soil is wet, following rain or irrigation, K e may be large. However, the sum of K cb and Ke can never exceed a maximum value, K c max, determined by the energy available for evapotranspiration at the soil surface. As the soil surface becomes drier, K e becomes smaller and falls to zero when no water is left for evaporation. The estimation of K e requires a daily water balance computation for the calculation of the soil water content remaining in the upper topsoil.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)

The dual coefficient approach requires more numerical calculations than the procedure using the single time-averaged K c coefficient. The dual procedure is best for real-time irrigation scheduling, for soil water balance computations, and for research studies where the effects of day-to-day variations in soil surface wetness and the resulting impacts on daily ETc, the soil water profile, and deep percolation fluxes are important. This is the case for high-frequency irrigation with micro-irrigation systems, namely drippers, or lateral move systems such as centre pivots and linear move systems.

The curve represents the changes in the crop coefficient over the length of the growing season. The shape of the curve represents the changes in the vegetation and ground cover during plant development and maturation that affect the ratio of ETc to ETo. From the curve, the K c coefficient and, hence, ET c can be derived for any period within the growing season.

That section is intended to draw the readers' attention to the need for accuracy in the determination of crop ET, thus discussing some critical aspects that affect measurement accuracy and the main pitfalls to be avoided. Over the last 25 years, hundreds of scientific papers have been published reporting crop ET measurements or estimates, and new (updated) Kc and K cb values for nearly all vegetable and field crops, as well as for fruit trees and vines.

text: K c values can be estimated using remote sensing based on field, aerial or satellite platforms, using empirical approaches based on spectral reflectance. Remote observations of Kcb and Kc are valuable when field information, such as planting dates or rates of vegetation development, are not well known. The estimation of K cb from reflectance-based vegetation indices (VI) is possible because of the generally close correspondence between vegetation amount and transpiration, where, as vegetation cover increases, leaf area increases and transpiration and K cb increase. The crop coefficients obtained from reflectance represent the actual ET conditions of the field (ideal or nonideal) and are termed K cb act RS and Kc act RS.

text: 154 Crop evapotranspiration Challenges with VI-based estimation of the single K c, that includes the evaporation component, is that spectral-reflectance-based observations generally cannot detect the presence of wet soil. Therefore, independent methods that use knowledge of specific wetting events are needed for estimating the evaporation from bare soil following precipitation and irrigation events. Wetting information is often difficult to obtain for specific fields, so that an empirically-based adjustment or coefficient is required to convert remotely-based Kcb into an equivalent Kc. Remotely-sensed Kcb act RS and Kc act RS may also have difficulty in capturing the reduced ET associated with water stress caused by short-term soil-water shortage because the short-term water stress is generally not indicated by a significant change in VI.

Under water shortage, a thermally-based method described in the next section may be required. Vegetation indices are mathematical combinations of surface reflectances obtained for different spectral bands. VIs are used to determine canopy biophysical variables such as the fraction of surface covered by vegetation (f c), crop height, LAI, and crop coefficients. A common VI is the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) which uses surface reflectance values obtained from the Near Infra-Red (NIR) band (~0.7–1.3 µm) and the Red band (~0.6–0.7 µm), thus where: rNIR - rred NDVI = −− −− −− −− − (5.3)rNIR + rred where r NIR surface reflectance in the near-infrared band (NIR) [ ], r red surface reflectance in the red band [ ].

It is important that NDVI is based on reflectance data rather than based on “radiance” data or “digital number” forms of data to maintain consistency in NDVI estimates over time. Another index widely applied is the Soil Adjusted Vegetation Index (SAVI) based on a similar definition as for NDVI but including a parameter L = 0.5 to reduce the influence of the variation in soil colour and brightness. A common usage is to estimate actual K cb directly from NDVI: Kcb= acbNDVI + bcb (5.4) where acb and bcb are generalized regression coefficients for estimating K cb, which may be specific to a crop type or a general crop group.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: described in Chapter 1. Over the last 25 years, various remote sensing approaches based on surface energy balance have been developed and widely used. RS-SEB methods take advantage of the physical fact that conversion of liquid water to vapour requires very substantial amounts of energy. This conversion of liquid to vapour during the evaporation process involves the same physical requirements whether the process is the transpiration of water from inside a plant leaf or the evaporation of water from a wet soil surface. The energy consumption by the conversion of liquid to vapour cools the evaporating surface, thus variations in surface temperature can be used to estimate the net radiation and sensible heat exchange at the surface. These estimates can then be used with the energy balance equation (Equation 1.1) to estimate the crop evapotranspiration.

In contrast, RS-SEB models produce estimates for total K c act by viewing the combined processes of transpiration and evaporation. As a result, RS-SEB models can be used to develop relationships between Kc act and VI that can then be employed using the more frequently available VI-based imagery.

Another use of paired RS-SEB and VI-based estimates is to estimate whether water shortage or drought is impacting crop production. This is done by noting periods when RS-SEB-based ET c act is lower than the VI-based ET c estimate. Determinations of reduced ET from water stress can be made difficult, however, by uncertainties, inaccuracies and biases in both modeling approaches. 5.5.6 Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for developing Kc data and precautions Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms can ingest data from remote sensing, weather stations, and ground measurements to learn complex relationships observed among different factors and ET rates.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: gest data from remote sensing, weather stations, and ground measurements to learn complex relationships observed among different factors and ET rates. AI models can help reduce uncertainty in ET estimations by learning from various data sources and accounting for land cover dynamics. This can lead to better water management practices and a more comprehensive understanding of the water cycle. However, AI can not directly recognize nor correct for faulty data that is ingested into the process. This is most true with Kc data, where substantial errors and biases in both ground-based and remote-sensing-based measurements can frequently occur. The application of powerful cognition and ingestion of large amounts of data does not offset nor cure the impacts of faulty, biased data. In fact, AI may magnify the influences of biased or faulty ET data on derived relationships.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)

The result can be a worse estimation of ET as compared to using direct K c curves or remotely-sensed ET procedures alone. Therefore, strong precautions should be taken, along with a required precursor involving a study of the physics of the evapotranspiration processes, impacts of agronomic practices and plant physiology. Some advantages of employing AI can include the classification of crop type in near real time. Using an ETo estimation method different than the standard FAO-PM ETo equation; 2. Using non-standard cultivation conditions, such as mulch, plastic tunnels, intercropping and greenhouses/screen houses; 3. Adopting crop management practices that may cause various types of stresses, e.g., relative to the use of fertilizers, chemicals, or wastewater; 4. Insufficient description of the experiments, namely of the plant density, height, and vigor, and the instrumentation used and its accuracy; 5. Crop growth stages are sometimes defined contradictorily relative to definitions adopted in FAO 56 and previously in FAO 24. Information provided in those papers may be sufficient relative to the objectives of the studies reported but is insufficient to provide for the transferability of reported Kc into different environments. These limitations oblige the user to conduct a careful review of published material to determine when derived Kc are only of local interest and application and/or represent non-standard experimental conditions.

ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc) ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc) This chapter deals with the calculation of crop evapotranspiration (ET c) under standard, pristine, non-stressed cropping conditions. No limitations are placed on crop growth and evapotranspiration from soil water and salinity stress, reduced crop density, pests and diseases, weed infestation, or low fertility and nutrients (see Figure 1.4 bis). ETc is determined by the crop coefficient approach whereby the effect of the various weather conditions are incorporated into ET o and the crop characteristics into the standard Kc coefficient: ETc = Kc ETo (6.1) The single K c coefficient incorporates crop characteristics and averaged effects of evaporation from the soil.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ard Kc coefficient: ETc = Kc ETo (6.1) The single K c coefficient incorporates crop characteristics and averaged effects of evaporation from the soil. For normal irrigation planning and management purposes, for the development of basic irrigation schedules, and for most hydrologic water balance studies, average crop coefficients are relevant and may be more convenient than the Kc computed on a daily time step using the dual K c approach where a separate crop transpiration and soil evaporation coefficient are determined (Chapter 7). Only when values for Kc are needed on a daily basis for specific fields of crops and/or for specific years, or where wetting frequencies from precipitation or irrigation are frequent or varied, must a separate transpiration and evaporation coefficient (Kcb + Ke) be considered. The calculation procedure for crop evapotranspiration, ET c, consists of: 1.

The calculation procedure for crop evapotranspiration, ET c, consists of: 1. identifying the crop growth stages, selecting the corresponding K c coefficients and determining their stage lengths; 2. adjusting the selected Kc coefficients for frequency of wetting or climatic conditions during each stage; 3. constructing the crop coefficient curve, i.e. providing to determine K c values for any period during the growing season; and 4. calculating ETc as the product of ETo and Kc. 6.1 CROP COEFFICIENTS.
