For all crops and vegetation, the value for K c ini that is listed is considered representative of the crop under typical irrigation water management, or under typical water supply conditions in cases of semi-natural non-planted grasslands (Table 6.4) and wetlands and riparian vegetation (Table 6.5). More accurate estimates of K c ini can be obtained by considering: a.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: planted grasslands (Table 6.4) and wetlands and riparian vegetation (Table 6.5). More accurate estimates of K c ini can be obtained by considering: a. The time interval between wetting events Evapotranspiration during the initial stage for annual crops is predominately in the form of evaporation from exposed soil due to low levels of vegetation. Therefore, accurate estimates for Kc ini should consider the frequency with which the soil surface is wetted during the initial period. Where the soil is frequently or continuously wet from irrigation, rain, or a natural surface or groundwater source, the evaporation from the soil surface can be considerable and K c ini will be large, e.g. flooded rice and wetlands vegetation. On the other hand, where the soil surface is dry, evaporation is restricted and the K c ini will be small (Table 5.1). b.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ice and wetlands vegetation. On the other hand, where the soil surface is dry, evaporation is restricted and the K c ini will be small (Table 5.1). b. Evaporation power of the atmosphere The value for K c ini is affected by the evaporating power of the atmosphere, i.e. which is indicated by ETo. The higher the evaporation power of the atmosphere, the quicker the soil will dry between water applications and the smaller the timeaveraged Kc ini will be for any particular period. In contrast, Kc ini will generally be high for inundated vegetation. c. Magnitude of the wetting events The amount of water available in the topsoil for evaporation and hence the time for the soil surface to dry is a function of the magnitude of the wetting event. Therefore, Kc ini will be smaller for light wetting events than for large wettings.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: urface to dry is a function of the magnitude of the wetting event. Therefore, Kc ini will be smaller for light wetting events than for large wettings. Depending on the time interval between wetting events, the magnitude of the wetting event and the evaporation power of the atmosphere, K c ini can vary between 0.10 and 1.15. In general, K c ini for flooded vegetation is not affected by precipitation events.

ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc) 6.2.2 Time interval between wetting events under irrigation For estimating K c ini, a mean time interval between wetting events is estimated by counting all rainfall and irrigation events occurring during the initial period that are greater than a few millimetres. Wetting events occurring on adjacent days can be counted as one event. The mean wetting interval is estimated by dividing the time length (days) of the initial period by the number of events (Example 6.1). EXAMPLE 6.1 Estimation of the time interval between wetting events from mean monthly rainfall data Estimate, from mean monthly rainfall data, the interval between rains during the rainy season for a station in a temperate climate (Paris, France: 50 mm/month), dry climate (Gafsa, Tunisia: 20 mm/month) and tropical climate (Calcutta, India: 300 mm/month).

Even where irrigation has not yet been developed, the mean interval between future irrigations should be estimated to obtain the required frequency of wetting necessary to keep the crop stress free. The interval might be as small as a few days for small vegetables, or just one or two days in the case of very frequent irrigation by drippers or center pivots, but up to a week or longer for surface irrigated cereals, however, depending on the climatic conditions.

Stage 1 is termed the "energy-limited" stage. During this stage, moisture is transported to the soil surface at a rate sufficient to supply the potential rate of evaporation (E so), which, in turn, is governed by energy availability at the soil surface. In this procedure, Eso is estimated from Eso = 1.15 ETo (6.5) where Eso is the potential rate of evaporation [mm d-1] and ETo is the mean ETo during the initial period [mm d -1].

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: timated from Eso = 1.15 ETo (6.5) where Eso is the potential rate of evaporation [mm d-1] and ETo is the mean ETo during the initial period [mm d -1]. The value 1.15 represents increased evaporation potential due to the low albedo of wet soil and the possibility of heat stored in the surface layer during previous dry periods. Stage 2 is termed the "soil water limited" stage, where hydraulic transport of subsurface water to the soil surface is unable to supply water at the potential evaporation rate. During stage 2, the soil surface appears partially dry and a portion of the evaporation occurs from below the soil surface. The energy required for subsurface evaporation is supplied by the transport of heat from the soil surface into the soil profile. The evaporation rate during stage 2 drying decreases as soil water content decreases as shown in Figure 6.4.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: m the soil surface into the soil profile. The evaporation rate during stage 2 drying decreases as soil water content decreases as shown in Figure 6.4. The evaporation rate can therefore be expressed as being proportional to the water remaining in the evaporation layer relative to the maximum depth of water that can be evaporated from the same soil layer during stage 2 drying. The background of this procedure is the same as for the computation of the evaporation coefficient Ke in the dual crop coefficient approach dealt with in Chapter 7, where further details are provided. The maximum total depth of water that can be evaporated from the surface soil layer is termed “total evaporable water” or TEW. In turn, the maximum total depth of water that can be evaporated during stage 1 is termed “readily evaporable water” or REW, which is discussed in Chapter 7.

More arid climates and conditions of greater wind speed will have higher values for K c mid. More humid climates and conditions of lower wind speed will have lower values for K c mid. These variations are caused by the effects of greater aerodynamic roughness for many vegetation types as compared to the standardized grass reference ET o.

text: 194 Crop evapotranspiration Equation 6.16 is valid for vegetable and field crops with mean plant heights up to around 3 m. For plant heights shorter than 0.1 m, vegetation will behave aerodynamically similar to grass reference and Equation 6.16 should not be applied. In case of fruit trees and vines, the correction for climate is less necessary unless transfers of K c mid values are done for very different climates because orchard architecture and crop training play a large role in plant's aerodynamic behaviour. Example values for h are listed in Tables 6.1 – 6.3 for various crops but the mean plant height can vary greatly with crop cultivar and cultural practices. Therefore, wherever possible, h should be obtained from general field observations. However, the presence of the 0.3 exponent in Equation 6.16 makes the equation relatively insensitive to small errors in the value used for h.

For frequent irrigation of crops (more frequently than every 3 days) and where the K c mid of Tables 6.1 – 6.2 is less than 1.0, the value can be replaced by approximately 1.1-1.3 to account for the additional combined effects of continuously wet soil, evaporation due to interception (sprinkler irrigation) and roughness of the vegetation, especially where the irrigation system moistens an important fraction of the soil surface (fw > 0.3). 6.4 CROP COEFFICIENT FOR THE END OF THE LATE SEASON STAGE (Kc end) Typical values for the crop coefficient at the end of the late season stage, K c end , are listed in Tables 6.1 – 6.5 for various agricultural crops and land covers.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: for the crop coefficient at the end of the late season stage, K c end , are listed in Tables 6.1 – 6.5 for various agricultural crops and land covers. The values given for Kc end reflect crop and water management practices particular to those crops and vegetation. If the crop is irrigated frequently until harvested fresh, the topsoil remains wet and the K c end value will be relatively high. On the other hand, crops that are allowed to senesce and dry out in the field before harvest receive less frequent irrigation or no irrigation at all during the late season stage. Consequently, both the soil surface and vegetation are dry and the value for K c end will be relatively small (Figure 6.6). Where the local water management and harvest timing practices are known to deviate from the typical ones, the user should make adequate adjustments to the values for Kc end.

text: 197 6. ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc) 6.5.2 Kc curves for forage crops Many crops grown for forage or hay are harvested/cut several times during the growing season. Each cut essentially terminates a “sub” growing cycle and an associated Kc curve, and initiates a new “sub” growing cycle and associated K c curve. The resulting K c curve for the entire growing season is the aggregation of a series of Kc curves associated with each sub-cycle. Figure 6.8 presents a K c curve for the entire growing season constructed for alfalfa grown for hay in southern Idaho, USA. A larger number of cuts may be considered for other locations depending on forage species, management of the forage or grassland and on climate (see Table 6.4).

text: Figure 6.8 shows four K c sub-cycles or cutting cycles: sub-cycle 1 follows greenup in the spring and the three other K c sub-cycles follow cuttings. These lengths were based on observations. In the southern Idaho climate, frosts terminate the growing season sometime in the fall, usually around day 280-290 of the year (early to mid-October). Cuttings create a ground surface with less than 10 percent vegetation cover. In climates with a very cold winter, cutting cycle 1 is often longer in duration than the following cycles due to lower air and soil temperatures during this period that reduce crop growth rates. The magnitudes of the K c values during the mid-season periods of each cutting cycle shown in Figure 6.8 vary from cycle to cycle due to adjusting the values for K c mid and Kc end for each cutting cycle period using Equations 6.16 and 6.19.

text: 198 Crop evapotranspiration 6.5.3 Kc mid when effects of individual cutting periods are averaged The user may wish to average the effects of cuttings for a forage crop over the course of the growing season. When cutting effects are averaged, then only a single value for Kc mid and only a single K c curve need to be employed for the whole growing season. When this is the case, a “single” Kc curve is constructed as in Figure 6.7, where only one midseason period is considered for the forage crop. The K c mid for this total midseason period must average the effects of grazing or hay cuttings. The value that is used for Kc mid is therefore an average of the K c curve for the time period starting at the first attainment of full cover and ending at the beginning of the final late season period, often near dormancy or frost.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: time period starting at the first attainment of full cover and ending at the beginning of the final late season period, often near dormancy or frost. The value used for Kc mid under these averaged conditions may be only about 80 percent of the K c value that represents full ground cover as in Figure 6.8. For example, for alfalfa hay, the average, full-season K c mid often is 1.05, whereas the Kc mid for an individual cutting period is 1.20. 6.6 CALCULATING ETc The Kc value for any period during the growing period can be graphically or numerically determined from the crop coefficient curve. Once the K c values have been derived, the crop evapotranspiration, ET c, can be calculated by multiplying the K c values by the corresponding ETo values.

A general procedure is to construct the Kc curve, overlay the curve with the lengths of the weeks, decades or months, and to derive graphically from the curve the K c value for the period under consideration (Figure 6.7). Since all decades have a duration of 10 days, adopting decades as time periods facilitates the derivation of K c and introduces little error in the calculation of ETc. The constructed Kc curve in Figure 6.9 relative to a dry bean crop (detailed in Box 6.3), was used to construct the curve in Figure 6.10.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: he construction of the crop coefficient curve requires the estimation of the lengths of the four stages that connect or represent the three Kc values. These stages are the initial (ini), development (dev), mid-season (mid) and late-season (end) as in Figure 6.7 and are defined in Chapter 5. In the absence of limiting factors such as water or nutrients, a crop’s development essentially depends on the temperature accumulation over time. Thus, the use of thermal time or growing degree days (GDD) to estimate the crop growth stage lengths has the merits of allowing one to adequately extrapolate from one year to the next, to diverse locations, and to take into consideration the impacts of climate change, particularly in temperature, on crop growth cycles. The use of GDD is important for studies relating to the assessment of climate change impacts on water and irrigation requirements.

ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc) The time of emergence of vegetation and the time of effective full cover can be estimated using sophisticated plant growth models or by cumulative GDD regression equations. While those models should be verified or validated for the local area or for a specific crop variety using local observations, the use of generalized GDD is a more simplified but reliable method that can be applied using simple computer software or spreadsheets. Crop growth and development of the K c curve is assumed to occur on any day when the mean air temperature exceeds a lower temperature threshold termed the base temperature (Tbase). The value of T base depends on the crop and variety. In conjunction with Tbase , when the mean daily air temperature exceeds an upper temperature threshold (Tupper), crop development is assumed to be limited to the GDD below that limit.

The length for each of the four growth stage periods is determined by summing GDD on a daily basis, using Equations 6.23. The number of days occurring can represent the length of the stage in days. The rate at which vegetation cover develops and the time at which it attains effective full cover are affected by weather conditions in general and by mean daily air temperature in particular. Therefore, the length of time between planting and effective full cover will vary with climate, latitude, elevation, and planting date.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: in particular. Therefore, the length of time between planting and effective full cover will vary with climate, latitude, elevation, and planting date. It will also vary with cultivar (crop variety). Generally, once the effective full cover for a plant canopy has been reached, the rate of further phenological development (flowering, fruit development, ripening, and senescence) is more dependent on plant genotype and less dependent on weather. The end of the mid-season and beginning of the late season is usually marked by senescence of leaves, often beginning with the lower leaves of plants. The length of the late season period may be relatively short (less than 10 days) for vegetation killed by frost (for example, maize at high elevations in latitudes > 40°N) or for agricultural crops that are harvested fresh (for example, table beets and small vegetables).

Moisture stress or other environmental stresses will usually accelerate the rate of crop maturation and can shorten the mid and late season growing periods, however affecting yields. Information in Table 6.11 refers to trusted observations only. It is possible to find more GDD in the literature for a large number of crops, but it is often not clear which values of Tbase and Tupper temperatures were used as compared to those in Table 6.10, what specific GDD calculations were applied, or if the crop growth stages were defined according to those in FAO56 as adopted in the current study. ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke) ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke) This chapter, complementing Chapter 6, deals with the calculation of crop evapotranspiration (ET c) under standard, non-stressed cropping conditions where no limitations are placed on crop growth or evapotranspiration. This chapter presents the procedure for predicting the effects of specific wetting events on the value of the crop coefficient Kc. The solution consists of splitting Kc into two separate coefficients, one for crop transpiration, i.e. the basal crop coefficient (K cb), and one for soil evaporation (K e): ETc = (Kcb + Ke) ETo (7.1) The dual crop coefficient approach is more complicated and more computationally intensive than the single crop coefficient approach (K c) dealt with in Chapter 6.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: p coefficient approach is more complicated and more computationally intensive than the single crop coefficient approach (K c) dealt with in Chapter 6. The procedure is conducted on a daily basis and is intended for applications using computers. It is recommended that the approach be followed when improved estimates for K c are needed, for example, to schedule irrigations for individual fields on a daily basis, mainly in case of incomplete cover crops, or to increase accuracy in hydrologic studies. The calculation procedure for crop evapotranspiration, ET c, consists of: 1. identifying the lengths of crop growth stages, and selecting the corresponding basal Kcb coefficients; 2. adjusting the selected Kcb coefficients for climatic conditions during the respective crop growth stage; 3.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: e corresponding basal Kcb coefficients; 2. adjusting the selected Kcb coefficients for climatic conditions during the respective crop growth stage; 3. constructing the basal crop coefficient curve (allowing one to determine Kcb values for any day or timestep during the crop season); 4. determining daily the soil evaporation coefficient Ke values for surface evaporation; and 5. calculating ETc as the product of ETo and (Kcb + Ke). 7.1 TRANSPIRATION COMPONENT (Kcb ETO) 7.1.1 Basal crop coefficient (Kcb) The basal crop coefficient (K cb) is defined as the ratio of the crop evapotranspiration over the grass reference evapotranspiration (ET c/ETo) when the soil surface is dry but transpiration is occurring at a potential rate, i.e. water is not limiting transpiration (Figure 5.3).

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ion (ET c/ETo) when the soil surface is dry but transpiration is occurring at a potential rate, i.e. water is not limiting transpiration (Figure 5.3). Therefore, “Kcb ETo” represents primarily the transpiration component of ETc and Kcb is often called transpiration coefficient. The K cb ETo does include a small, residual diffusive evaporation component supplied by soil water below the dry surface and by soil water from beneath dense vegetation. As the K c values of Chapter 6 include averaged effects of evaporation from the soil surface, the Kcb values lie below the Kc values as illustrated in Figure 5.7 and a separate table for Kcb is required. Recommended values for Kcb are listed in Tables 7.1 to 7.3 for the same crops listed in Tables 6.1 to 6.3. Where the topsoil is wet, following rain or irrigation, K e is maximal. Where the soil surface is dry, K e is small and even zero if no water remains near the soil surface for evaporation. Two calculation procedures are presented, the FAO56 original and the skin layer evaporation approach, which consists of a refinement of the former to increase accuracy, mainly for small wetting depths. 7.2.1 FAO 56 original calculation procedure Where the soil is wet, evaporation from the soil occurs at the maximum rate. However, the crop coefficient (K c = K cb + K e) can never exceed a maximum value, K c max.

K c max ranges from about 1.05 to 1.30 when using the grass reference ET o: where h mean maximum plant height during the period of calculation (initial, development, mid-season, or late-season) [m], K cb basal crop coefficient, max( ) maximum value of the parameters in braces { } that are separated by the comma. Equation 7.4 ensures that K c max is always greater than or equal to the sum K cb + 0.05. This requirement suggests that wet soil will always increase the value for K cb by 0.05 following complete wetting of the soil surface, even during periods of full ground cover.

text: hat wet soil will always increase the value for K cb by 0.05 following complete wetting of the soil surface, even during periods of full ground cover. A value of 1.2 is used for Kc max in Equation 7.4 because of the effect of increased aerodynamic roughness of surrounding crops during development, mid-season and late season growth stages that can increase the turbulent transfer of vapour from the exposed soil surface. The “1.2” coefficient also reflects the impact of the reduced albedo of wet soil and the contribution of heat stored in dry soil prior to the wetting event. All of these factors can contribute to an increased evaporation relative to the reference. The “1.2” coefficient in Equation 7.4 represents the effects of wetting intervals that are greater than 3 or 4 days.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ration relative to the reference. The “1.2” coefficient in Equation 7.4 represents the effects of wetting intervals that are greater than 3 or 4 days. If irrigation or precipitation events are more frequent, for example daily or every two days, then the soil has less opportunity to absorb heat between wettings, and the “1.2” coefficient in Equation 7.4 can be reduced, e.g. to about 1.1. The time step to compute K c max may vary from daily to monthly. Soil evaporation reduction coefficient (Kr) Soil evaporation from the exposed soil can be assumed to take place in two stages: an energy limiting stage, and a falling rate stage (Figure 7.2). When the soil surface is wet, Kr is 1.0. When the water content in the upper soil becomes limiting, Kr decreases and becomes zero when the total amount of water that can be evaporated from the topsoil is depleted.

During stage 1 of the drying process, the soil surface remains wet and it is assumed that evaporation from soil exposed to the atmosphere will occur at the maximum rate limited only by energy availability at the soil surface.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: s assumed that evaporation from soil exposed to the atmosphere will occur at the maximum rate limited only by energy availability at the soil surface. This stage holds until the cumulative depth of evaporation, D e, is such that the hydraulic properties of the upper soil become limiting, and water cannot be transported to the soil surface at a rate that can supply the potential demand. During stage 1 drying, K r = 1.0. The cumulative depth of evaporation, De, at the end of stage 1 drying is REW (readily evaporable water, which is the maximum depth of water that can be evaporated from the topsoil layer without restriction during stage 1). The depth normally ranges from 5 to 12 mm and is generally highest for medium and fine textured soils. Typical values for REW are given in Table 7.5.

Exposed and wetted soil fraction few: calculation procedure In crops with incomplete ground cover, evaporation from the soil often does not occur uniformly over the entire surface but is greater between plants where exposure to sunlight occurs and where more air ventilation is able to transport vapour from the soil surface to above the canopy. This is especially true where only part of the soil surface is wetted by irrigation.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: le to transport vapour from the soil surface to above the canopy. This is especially true where only part of the soil surface is wetted by irrigation. It is recognized that both the location and the fraction of the soil surface exposed to sunlight change to some degree with the time of the day and depending on row orientation. The procedure presented here predicts a general averaged fraction of the soil surface from which the majority of evaporation occurs. Diffusive evaporation from the soil beneath the crop canopy is very small and assumed to be largely included in the basal Kcb coefficient.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ion occurs. Diffusive evaporation from the soil beneath the crop canopy is very small and assumed to be largely included in the basal Kcb coefficient. Where the complete soil surface is wetted, as by precipitation or sprinkler, then the fraction of soil surface from which most evaporation occurs, f ew, is essentially defined as (1−fc), where fc is the average fraction of soil surface covered by vegetation and (1−fc) is the approximate fraction of soil surface that is exposed (Example 7.3). However, for irrigation systems where only a fraction of the ground surface is wetted, few must be limited to fw, the fraction of the soil surface wetted by irrigation (Figure 7.3).

text: where only a fraction of the ground surface is wetted, few must be limited to fw, the fraction of the soil surface wetted by irrigation (Figure 7.3). Therefore, few is calculated as: few = min (1 - fc, fw) (7.7) where 1 − fc average exposed soil fraction not covered (or shaded) by vegetation [0.01-1], f w average fraction of soil surface wetted by irrigation or precipitation [0.01-1]. The “min()” function selects the lowest value of the “1 − f c” and “f w” values. Figure 7.3 illustrates the relation of f ew to (1 − fc) and fw. The limitation imposed by Equation 7.7 assumes that the fraction of soil wetted by irrigation occurs within the fraction of soil exposed to sunlight and wind. This is generally the case, except perhaps with drip irrigation (Figure 7.3). In the case of drip irrigation, the majority of soil wetted by irrigation is beneath the canopy and shaded.

More complex models may be required to more accurately estimate total evaporation from the soil. The value for f w may need to be reduced to about one-half to one-third of that given in Table 7.6 to account for the effects of shading of emitters by the plant canopy (Example 7.6). A general simple approach could be to multiply tabled f w by [1 − (2/3)fc] for drip irrigation. fw: fraction of soil surface wetted by irrigation or precipitation Table 7.6 presents typical values for f w. Nevertheless, users should preferably observe that fraction instead of just adopting the tabulated values.

Where a mixture of irrigation and precipitation occurs within the same drying period or on the same day, the value for fw should be based on a weighted average of the fw for precipitation (fw = 1) and the fw for the irrigation system. The weighting should be approximately proportional to the infiltration depths from each water source.

text: 237 7. ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke) This equation should be used with some caution and validated from local field observations. Kc min is the minimum crop coefficient for dry bare agricultural soil when transpiration and evaporation from the soil are near baseline (diffusive) levels. K c min ≈ 0.15 - 0.20 is recommended. The value of Kc min is an integral part of all Kcb coefficients. Kc min ordinarily has the same value as the Kcb ini used for annual crops under nearly bare soil conditions (0.15 - 0.20). The reduction of the value for K c min for very dry soils is described in Chapter 8. Equation 7.8 assumes that the value for Kcb is largely affected by the fraction of soil surface covered by vegetation. This is a good assumption for most vegetation and conditions.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)

The “1+0.5h” exponent in the equation represents the effect of plant height on shading the soil surface and in increasing the value for Kcb given a specific value for fc. The user should limit the difference Kcb - Kc min to ≥ 0.01 for numerical stability. The value for fc will change daily as Kcb changes. Therefore, the above equation 7.8 is applied daily (see Examples 7.4, 7.5 and 7.6 where Kcb is computed for, respectively, sprinkler, surface and drip irrigation). ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke) 7.2.2 Calculation procedure using the skin layer approach The use of the fraction of the time step calculation (day or hour) that resides in stage 1 evaporation, Astage 1, is an extension to the original FAO 56 approach to provide more precise definition of the transition from stage 1 to stage 2 drying during a time step. The improved definition can be important when using daily calculation time steps, especially for coarse soils having small REW. The skin layer approach improves daily estimates for Ke when the depths of wetting events are small. Small depths of wetting occur when precipitation or sprinkler irrigation events are less than about 10 mm.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: hen the depths of wetting events are small. Small depths of wetting occur when precipitation or sprinkler irrigation events are less than about 10 mm. If small wetting events occur when the total 100 to 150 mm deep soil evaporation layer is dry (De, i ~ TEW), then much of the added water remains close to the top of the soil evaporation layer and tends to evaporate quickly. The original procedure implicitly assumes that small water additions are mixed throughout the soil evaporation layer. As a result, the original procedure tends to extend the evaporation of the added water over a number of days at a relatively low rate due to small values calculated for K r. In contrast, the skin evaporation extension retains water close to the surface in the REW zone, so the Es rate is generally higher in value and shorter in time.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: t, the skin evaporation extension retains water close to the surface in the REW zone, so the Es rate is generally higher in value and shorter in time. The skin evaporation extension tends to reproduce the relatively short-lived and higher magnitude Stage 1 spikes of Es and Ke that are observed in field monitoring. It is important to note that the skin evaporation extension and the original K e computation procedure will generally produce similar total depths of evaporation over an extended period. This is because both methods adhere to a water balance of the topsoil and to the conservation of mass. The difference is in the duration and magnitude of Ke. These differences in daily estimates may not matter when estimating total water consumption (ET) over extended periods.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)

The skin evaporation extension may be most important when comparing ET estimates to ground or remote sensing observations where the timing and magnitude of evaporation on a specific day is important. The skin evaporation extension can be applied to daily or hourly calculation timesteps. As for the original calculation procedure, K c max is determined by the energy available for evapotranspiration at the soil and plant surfaces, thus resulting K cb + K e ≤ K c max or Ke ≤ Kc max − Kcb.

This is quite common where light wetting events wet only the upper skin of soil and evaporate off relatively quickly. Those events may be less effective in replenishing the root zone. text: 246 Crop evapotranspiration 7.2.3 Daily calculation of Ke Limits on De, i By assuming that the topsoil is at field capacity following heavy rain or irrigation, the minimum value for the depletion D e,i is zero. As the soil surface dries, D e,i increases and in the absence of any wetting event will steadily reach its maximum value TEW (Equation 7.5). At that moment no water is left for evaporation in the upper soil layer, Kr becomes zero, and the value for De,i remains at TEW until the topsoil is wetted once again. The limits imposed on D e,i are consequently: 0 ≤ De, i ≤ TEW (7.15) Initial depletion To initiate the water balance for the evaporating layer, the user can assume that the topsoil is near field capacity following a heavy rain or irrigation, i.e. D e,i−1 = 0.

Precipitation and runoff Pi is equivalent to daily precipitation. Daily precipitation in amounts less than about 0.2 ETo is normally entirely evaporated and can usually be ignored in the K e and water balance calculations. However, small amounts of precipitation are also correctly dealt with by Equation 7.11 – 7.15. Light precipitation events will generally have little or no runoff.

text: ll amounts of precipitation are also correctly dealt with by Equation 7.11 – 7.15. Light precipitation events will generally have little or no runoff. The amount of rainfall lost by runoff depends on: the intensity of rainfall; the slope of land; the soil type, its hydraulic conditions and antecedent moisture content; and the land use and cover. For general situations where many irrigated fields have small slopes, ROi can be assumed to be zero or can be accounted for by considering only a certain percentage of Pi. This is especially true for the water balance of the topsoil layer, because almost all precipitation events that would have intensities or depths large enough to cause runoff would probably still replenish the water content of the topsoil layer to field capacity. Therefore, the impact of the runoff component can be ignored.

Irrigation Ii is generally expressed as a depth of water that is equivalent to the mean infiltrated irrigation depth distributed over the entire field. Therefore, the value I i/fw is used to describe the actual concentration of the irrigation volume over the fraction of the soil that is wetted (Figure 6.3). Evaporation Evaporation beneath the vegetation canopy is assumed to be included in K cb and is therefore not explicitly quantified. The computed evaporation is fully concentrated in the exposed, wetted topsoil. The evaporation Ei is given by Ke ETo. Transpiration Except for shallow rooted crops (i.e. where the depth of the maximum rooting zone is < 0.5 to 0.6 m), the amount of transpiration from the evaporating soil layer (T ew) is small and can be ignored (i.e. Tew = 0). In addition, for row crops, most of the water extracted by the roots may be extracted from beneath the vegetation canopy. Therefore, Tew from the few fraction of soil surface can be assumed to be zero in these cases.

T ew can, therefore, generally be ignored. The effects of the reduction of the water content of the evaporating soil layer due to Tew can be accounted for if needed by decreasing the value for Ze, for example from 0.15 to 0.12 m or from 0.10 to 0.08 m.

text: 255 8. ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions Forces acting on the soil water decrease its potential energy and make it less available for plant root extraction. When the soil is wet, the water has a high potential energy, is relatively free to move and is easily taken up by the plant roots. In dry soils, the water has a low potential energy and is strongly bound by capillary and absorptive forces to the soil matrix and is less easily extracted by the crop. When the potential energy of the soil water drops below a threshold value, the crop is said to be water stressed. The effects of soil water stress are described by multiplying the basal crop coefficient by the water stress coefficient, K s: ETc act = (Ks Kcb+Ke ) ET o (8.1) For soil water limiting conditions, K s < 1. Where there is no soil water deficit, K s = 1.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: stress coefficient, K s: ETc act = (Ks Kcb+Ke ) ET o (8.1) For soil water limiting conditions, K s < 1. Where there is no soil water deficit, K s = 1. Ks describes the effect of water stress on crop transpiration. Where the single crop coefficient is used, the effect of water stress is incorporated into K c as: ETc act = K s Kc ETo = Kc act ETo (8.2) Salinity also decreases the potential energy of the soil water and makes water more difficult to be extracted by the plant roots. Thus Equations 8.1 and 8.2 also apply when salinity of the soil and the irrigation water affect extraction by the roots, with Ks becoming a salinity and water stress coefficient, i.e. salinity and water stress combine in Ks < 1 as developed later in this chapter.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: roots, with Ks becoming a salinity and water stress coefficient, i.e. salinity and water stress combine in Ks < 1 as developed later in this chapter. Because the water stress coefficient impacts only crop transpiration, rather than evaporation from soil, the application of K s using Equation 8.1 is generally more accurate than its application using Equation 8.2. However, in situations where evaporation from soil is not a large component of ET c, the use of Equation 8.2 will provide quite reasonable results. 8.1 SOIL WATER AVAILABILITY 8.1.1 Total available water (TAW) Soil water availability refers to the capacity of a soil to retain water available to plants. After heavy rainfall or irrigation, the soil will drain until field capacity is reached.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: o the capacity of a soil to retain water available to plants. After heavy rainfall or irrigation, the soil will drain until field capacity is reached. Field capacity is the amount of water that a well-drained soil should hold against gravitational forces, or the amount of water remaining when downward drainage has markedly decreased. In the absence of water supply, the water content in the root zone decreases as a result of water uptake by the crop. As water uptake progresses, the remaining water is held to the soil particles with greater force, lowering its potential energy and making it more difficult for the plant to extract it. Eventually, a point is reached where the crop can no longer extract the remaining water. The water uptake becomes zero when wilting point is reached. Wilting point is the water content at which plants will permanently wilt.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)

TAW is the amount of water that a crop can extract from its root zone, and its magnitude depends on the type of soil and the rooting depth. Typical ranges for field capacity and wilting point are listed in Table 7.5 for various soil texture classes. Ranges of the maximum effective rooting depth for various crops are given in Tables 6.1 through 6.3.

Ranges of the maximum effective rooting depth for various crops are given in Tables 6.1 through 6.3. 8.1.2 Readily available water (RAW) Although water is theoretically available in the root zone until the wilting point is attained, the crop water uptake is reduced well before the wilting point is reached. Where the soil is sufficiently wet, the soil supplies water fast enough to meet the atmospheric demand of the crop, and water uptake equals ET c. As the soil water content decreases, water becomes more strongly bound to the soil matrix and is more difficult to extract. When the soil water content drops below a threshold value, soil water can no longer be transported quickly enough toward the roots to respond to the transpiration demand and the crop begins to experience stress.

The fraction of TAW that a crop can extract from the root zone without suffering water stress is the readily available soil water: RAW = p TAW (8.4) where RAW the readily available soil water in the root zone [mm], p average fraction of total available soil water (TAW) that can be depleted from the root zone before moisture stress (reduction in ET) occurs [0-1]. Values for p are listed in Table 8.1 through 8.4 respectively for vegetable, field, woody fruit and grass crops. The factor p differs from one crop to another. The factor p normally varies from 0.20 for very shallow rooted plants at high rates of ET c (> 8 mm d-1) to 0.70 for deep rooted plants at low rates of ETc (< 3 mm d-1).

A value of 0.50 for p is commonly used for many field crops, a lower value is often used for vegetable crops, and a higher value is used for woody crops with large roots and to grasses, generally less susceptible to water stress. For many woody crops there is little information and, thus, indicative values are given for each group. The p value is small for frequent and very frequent irrigation, and larger for surface irrigation where time intervals between irrigation events are large. Therefore, the values of p listed in Table 8.1 through 8.4 are for large time intervals between irrigation events, thus for surface irrigation. Users may reduce the tabulated p values for the irrigation method that they are using.

The rate of root water uptake is, in fact, influenced more directly by the potential energy level of the soil water (soil matric potential and the associated hydraulic conductivity) than by water content alone. As a certain soil matric potential corresponds in different soil types with different soil water contents, the value for p is also a function of the soil type.

Generally, it can be stated that for fine textured soils (clay) the p values listed in Table 8.1 can be reduced by 5-10 percent, while for more coarse textured soils (sand), they can be increased by 5-10 percent. RAW is similar to the term Management Allowed Depletion (MAD) often used in irrigation management practice. However, values for MAD are influenced by management and economic factors in addition to the physical factors influencing p. Generally, MAD < RAW where there is risk aversion or uncertainty, and MAD > RAW where plant moisture deficit is an intentional part of soil water management.

text: urban 0.50 8.2 WATER STRESS COEFFICIENT (KS) The effects of soil water stress on crop ET are described by reducing the value for the crop coefficient. This is accomplished by multiplying the crop coefficient by the water stress coefficient, Ks (Equations 8.1 and 8.2). Water content in the root zone can also be expressed by the root zone depletion, Dr, i.e. the water consumed relative to field capacity. At field capacity, the root zone depletion is zero (D r = 0). When soil water is consumed by evapotranspiration the depletion is increasing, and stress will be induced when D r reaches RAW.

When the root zone depletion exceeds RAW (the water content drops below the threshold θt), the root zone depletion is high enough to limit evapotranspiration to less than potential values and the crop evapotranspiration begins to decrease in proportion to the amount of water remaining in the root zone (Figure 8.2 and Example 8.2).

Schematically (Figure 8.4), the root zone can be presented by means of a container in which the water content may fluctuate. To express the water content as root zone depletion is useful. It makes the adding and subtracting of losses and gains straightforward as the various parameters of the soil water budget are usually expressed in terms of water depth. Rainfall, irrigation, and capillary rise of groundwater towards the root zone add water to the root zone and decrease the root zone depletion.

text: 268 Crop evapotranspiration 8.3.4 Capillary rise (CR) The amount of water transported upwards by capillary rise from the water table to the root zone depends on the soil type, the water table depth below the ground surface (WTD), the crop evapotranspiration and the wetness of the root zone. However, CR is primarily influenced by WTD as explained in Box 8.1. The wetness of the root zone is represented by the actual soil water storage in the root zone (W a). When WTD is close to the root zone, especially if ET c act is high, upward fluxes are expected to occur even when the soil water storage is close to field capacity. Under such WTD and ETc act conditions, CR fluxes are important, especially in silty soils. These fluxes depend mainly on WTD and may start at different water table depths and various values of soil water storage, depending on the soil type.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: These fluxes depend mainly on WTD and may start at different water table depths and various values of soil water storage, depending on the soil type. This storage is termed the critical soil water storage (W c) [mm] and varies between the soil water storage at field capacity and the storage when the soil water content corresponds to the depletion fraction p for no stress (Table 8.1). The critical soil water storage may be calculated as: Wc = a1 WTDb1 (8.9) where WTD water table depth [m], a 1 soil water storage for the maximum root depth at field capacity [mm], b 1 adjustment parameter depending on soil physical characteristics, namely soil texture [-] (Table 8.5). ETc act progressively depletes the soil water storage, and the upward fluxes attain a maximum value, called the potential capillary flux (CR max), which is mainly dependent on WTD and less dependent on ET c act.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: e upward fluxes attain a maximum value, called the potential capillary flux (CR max), which is mainly dependent on WTD and less dependent on ET c act. For shallow water table depths (WTD ≤ 3 m), a steady soil moisture profile is formed when CR max is reached and the soil water storage assumes an almost constant value, termed the steady soil water storage (W s), that is almost independent of ETc. In contrast, when the water table is deeper (WTD > 3 m), the upward flow may no longer be sufficient to sustain ETc act, which continuously decreases due to increased soil water deficit. Under such conditions steady soil water storage (W s) varies with ET c act and CR max is only reached when the soil water storage is low.

A threshold value for WTD exists, so that when WTD is greater than the threshold, CRmax no longer increases. This critical WTD (WTD c), corresponds to the water table depth when CR reaches the virtually constant value CRmax, i.e., the maximum potential groundwater contribution. It has been observed that the critical water table depth mainly depends on the ETc act: WTDc =a3 ETc act + b3 When ETc act ≤ 4 mm d-1 (8.11a) WTDc = 1.4 m When ETc act > 4 mm d-1 (8.11b) where indicative values for a 3 and b3 are given in Table 8.5. When WTD > WTD c, the flux CRmax decreases with WTD according to a power law.

In this simple procedure it is assumed that the soil water content is at θFC within the same day of the wetting event, so that the depletion D r, i in Equation 8.7 becomes zero. text: 274 Crop evapotranspiration 8.4 FORECASTING OR ALLOCATING IRRIGATIONS Irrigation is required when rainfall is insufficient to compensate for the soil water used as evapotranspiration. The primary objective of irrigation is to apply water at the right time and in the right amount. The timing and depth of future irrigations can be planned by calculating the soil water balance of the root zone on a daily basis (Equation 8.7). To avoid crop water stress, irrigations should be applied before or at the moment when the readily available soil water is depleted so that Dr,i is always ≤ RAW. To avoid deep percolation losses that may leach valuable nutrients out of the root zone, the net irrigation depth should be smaller than or equal to the root zone depletion (I i ≤ Dr,i) unless leaching of salts is needed.

The selection of values to be used must be done carefully because the crop response to water stress depends on the crop cultivars, which may have a wide range of variation as tabulated for various crops. Recognizing the degree of tolerance to moisture stress for the cultivars being used is recommended. Also to be considered is the effect of cumulative stress and its timing during the season because stress impacts may be different when crops recover from stress during the first part of the cycle, or are subjected to stress at more critical stages such as flowering or fruiting. For the crops not included in Table 8.7, users are advised to consider K y for crops of the same family or that have similar behaviour.

Nevertheless, care must be used for this purpose. 8.6 STRESS EFFECTS OF SOIL SALINITY Salts in the soil water solution can reduce evapotranspiration by making soil water less "available" for plant root extraction. Salts have an affinity for water and hence additional force is required for the crop to extract water from a saline soil. The presence of salts in the soil water solution reduces the total potential energy of the soil water solution. In addition, some salts may cause toxic effects in plants and can reduce plant metabolism, growth and yield. A function is presented hereafter that predicts the reduction in evapotranspiration caused by the salinity of soil water.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: etabolism, growth and yield. A function is presented hereafter that predicts the reduction in evapotranspiration caused by the salinity of soil water. The function is derived by combining yield-salinity equations from the FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No29 with yield-ET equations from FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No33. The resulting equation provides a first approximation to the reduction in evapotranspiration expected under various salinity conditions. 8.6.1 Salinity impacts and crops tolerance There is evidence that crop yield and transpiration are not as sensitive to low osmotic potential as they are to low matric potential. Under saline conditions, many plants are able to partially compensate for the low osmotic potential of the soil water by

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: 280 Crop evapotranspiration building up higher internal solute contents. This is done by absorbing ions from the soil solution and by synthesizing organic osmolytes. Both of these reactions reduce the impact of osmotic potential on water availability. However, the synthesis of organic osmolytes does require the expenditure of metabolic energy. Therefore, plant growth is often reduced under saline conditions. The reduced plant growth impacts transpiration by reducing ground cover, and a further reduction in transpiration is sometimes additionally caused by partial stomatal closure. Other impacts of salts in the soil include direct sodium and chloride toxicities and induced nutrient deficiencies. These deficiencies reduce plant growth by reducing the rate of leaf elongation, the enlargement, and the division of cells in leaves. The modality depends on the method of irrigation.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: rowth by reducing the rate of leaf elongation, the enlargement, and the division of cells in leaves. The modality depends on the method of irrigation. With sprinkler irrigation, adsorption of sodium and chloride through the leaf can result in toxic conditions for all crop species. With surface or trickle irrigation, direct toxic conditions generally occur only in vine and tree crops; however, high levels of sodium can induce calcium deficiencies for all crop species. Since salt concentration changes as the soil water content changes, soil salinity is normally measured and expressed on the basis of the electrical conductivity of the saturation extract of the soil (ECe). The ECe is defined as the electrical conductivity of the soil water solution after the addition of a sufficient quantity of distilled water to bring the soil water content to saturation.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: conductivity of the soil water solution after the addition of a sufficient quantity of distilled water to bring the soil water content to saturation. ECe is typically expressed in deciSiemens per meter (dS m-1). Under optimum management conditions, crop yields remain at potential levels until a specific, threshold electrical conductivity of the saturation soil water extract (EC e threshold) is reached. If the average EC e of the root zone increases above this critical threshold value, the yield is presumed to begin to decrease linearly in proportion to the increase in salinity. The rate of decrease in yield with increase in salinity is usually expressed as a slope, b, having units of % reduction in yield per dS m -1 increase in ECe. All plants do not respond to salinity in a similar manner; some crops can produce acceptable yields at much higher soil salinity levels than others.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: . All plants do not respond to salinity in a similar manner; some crops can produce acceptable yields at much higher soil salinity levels than others. This is because some crops are better able to make the needed osmotic adjustments that enable them to extract more water from a saline soil, or they may be more tolerant of some of the toxic effects of salinity. Salt tolerance for many agricultural crops is provided in the FAO Irrigation and Drainage Papers No. 33 and 48. The EC e threshold and slope b from these and other sources are listed in Tables 8.8 through 8.11, respectively for vegetable, field, fruit tree and vine, and grass and forage crops. The data serve only as a guideline - tolerance vary depending on climate, soil conditions and cultural practices. Crops are often less tolerant during germination and seedling stage.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: ne - tolerance vary depending on climate, soil conditions and cultural practices. Crops are often less tolerant during germination and seedling stage. As can be observed from the data in these Tables, there is an 8 to 11-fold range in salt tolerance of agricultural crops. The effect of soil salinity on yield and crop evapotranspiration is hence crop specific. The EC e threshold and b parameters in Tables 8.8 through 8.11 were determined primarily in research experiments using nearly steady-state irrigation where soil water contents were maintained at levels close to field capacity. However, under most types of irrigation scheduling for sprinkler and surface irrigation, the soil water content is typically depleted to well below field capacity, so that the EC of the soil water solution, EC sw, increases prior to irrigation, even though the EC of the saturation extract does not change.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: pacity, so that the EC of the soil water solution, EC sw, increases prior to irrigation, even though the EC of the saturation extract does not change. The increased salt concentration in the soil water solution reduces the osmotic potential of the soil water solution (it becomes more negative), so that the plant must expend more metabolic energy and may exert more mechanical force to absorb water. In addition, the metabolic and toxic effects of salts on plants may become more pronounced as the soil dries and concentrations increase. However, the variation in soil water content during an irrigation interval has not been found to strongly influence crop evapotranspiration. This is because of the rise of soil water content to levels that are above that experienced under steady state irrigation early in a long irrigation interval.

In addition, the distribution of salts in the root zone under low frequency irrigation can reduce salinity impacts during the first portion of the irrigation interval. Also, under high frequency irrigation of the soil surface, soil evaporation losses are higher. Consequently, given the same application depth, the leaching fraction is reduced. For these reasons, the length of irrigation interval and the change in EC of soil water during the interval have usually not been found to be factors in the reduction of ET, given that the same depths of water are infiltrated into the root zone over time.

text: 285 8. ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions Increased evaporation (K e) under high frequency irrigation of the soil surface may counteract reductions in K c caused by stress due to high EC e of the root zone. Under these conditions, the total K c and ET c are not very different from the non-saline, standard conditions under less frequent irrigation, even though crop yields and crop transpiration are reduced. Because of this, under saline conditions, the K s reducing factor should only be applied with the dual K c approach. The effects of soil salinity and water stress are generally additive in their impacts on crop evapotranspiration. Therefore, the same yield-ET functions may hold for both water shortage induced stress and for salinity induced stress.

Therefore, the same yield-ET functions may hold for both water shortage induced stress and for salinity induced stress. 8.6.2 Yield-Salinity relationship A widely practiced approach for predicting the reduction in crop yield due to salinity has been described in the FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No29. The approach presumes that, under optimum management conditions, crop yields remain at potential levels until a specific, threshold electrical conductivity of the soil water solution is reached. When salinity increases beyond this threshold, crop yields are presumed to decrease linearly in proportion to the increase in salinity. The soil water salinity is expressed as the electrical conductivity of the saturation extract, ECe. In equation form, the salinity response function is a linear equation.

text: 289 8. ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions Limitations Because the impact of salinity on plant growth and yield and on crop evapotranspiration is a time-integrated process, generally only the seasonal value for Ky is used in predicting the reduction in evapotranspiration. For many crops, the seasonal K y is nearly 1.0 (Table 8.7). For crops where K y is unknown, the user may assume K y = 1 in Equations 8.19 and 8.25, or may select a K y relative to a crop type that has similar behaviour. Equations 8.19 and 8.25 are suggested as approximate estimates of salinity impacts on ET, and represent the general effects of salinity on evapotranspiration as occurring over an extended period of time (as measured in weeks or months). These equations are not expected to be accurate for predicting ET c act for specific days.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: n extended period of time (as measured in weeks or months). These equations are not expected to be accurate for predicting ET c act for specific days. Nor do they include other complicating effects such as specific ion toxicity. Application of Equations 8.19 and 8.25 presumes that the EC e represents the average ECe for the root zone. The equations presented may not be valid at high salinity, where the linear relationships between EC e, crop yield and K s may not hold. The use of Equations 8.19 and 8.25 should usually be restricted to EC e < EC threshold + 50/b. In addition, care is required when the equations predict Ya = 0 before Ks = 0 when Ky > 1 and vice versa. As indicated earlier, a reduction in ETc in the presence of soil salinity is often partially caused by reduced plant size and fraction of ground cover. These effects are largely included in the coefficient values.

For example, the FAO-29 leaching formula LR = EC iw / (5 EC e – EC iw) predicts the leaching requirement when approximately a 40-30-20-10 percent water extraction pattern occurs from the upper to lower quarters of the root zone prior to irrigation. EC iw is the electrical conductivity of the irrigation water.

This example uses the same data set that were used in the case study of Box 8.1; however, only two examples were selected. The observed ETc act, soil water content and CR data were measured using five static water-table lysimeters. The ET c act partitioning was estimated using the soil water balance model SIMDualKc after proper calibration with observed soil water content data.

Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation Actual crop ET (ETc act) refers to both agricultural and natural vegetation including nonpristine agricultural vegetation. The latter is defined, in the usage here, as vegetation having less than perfect growing conditions or stand characteristics (i.e. relatively poor conditions of density, height, leaf area, fertility, vitality and biomass yield) as compared to “pristine” maximal yield conditions. Non-typical cropping conditions are also included and refer to types or arrangements of agricultural crops that are not listed or described in Tables 6.1 to 6.4 and 7.1 to 7.3. However, non-typical cropping conditions are mainly dealt with in Chapter 10.

The approach whereby a crop is characterized by a crop coefficient, K c, and the crop evapotranspiration is given by the product of K c and the reference evapotranspiration ETo, provides a simple and convenient way of also characterizing the evapotranspiration from natural vegetation and for diverse non-typical cultivation practices. This chapter presents procedures for estimating actual K c and K cb values for natural vegetation and for agricultural vegetation independent of having K c and K cb values available.

Two procedures that can be used to adjust the basal crop coefficient (Kcb mid act) for sparse vegetation are presented in this section. In these approaches, Kcb mid act is estimated either from LAI or from the effective ground cover and height. After the determination of K cb mid act , the soil evaporation coefficient, K e, should be determined as described in Chapter 7 to obtain the crop coefficient for the mid-season stage: Kc mid act = Kcb mid act + Ke. Even where the estimated Kcb mid act is small, the total Kc mid act (= Kcb mid act + Ke) following precipitation may sometimes be as high or higher than the Kc for pristine vegetation due to soil evaporation from among sparse vegetation.

Some guidelines for the estimation of Kc act are given in the following sections. The single crop coefficient can also be derived from the adjusted Kcb by considering the frequency of soil wetting, i.e., Kc mid act = Kcb mid act + 0.05 for infrequent wetting and K c mid act = Kcb mid act + 0.10 for wettings of up to once a week. text: 296 Crop evapotranspiration 9.2.2 Estimation of Kcb mid from Leaf Area Index (LAI) Natural vegetation typically has less leaf area or fraction of ground cover than does agricultural vegetation that has been developed for full ground cover and for soil water conditions favouring vigorous growth. This is especially true in semi-arid and arid climates. BOX 9.1 Measuring and estimating LAI LAI is defined as the area of leaves per area of underlying ground surface averaged over a large area. Only one side of the leaves is counted. LAI can be measured directly by harvesting all green healthy leaves from vegetation over a measured or prescribed area, for example, 1 m 2 or 10 m 2, and then measuring and summing the areas of individual leaves using photometric methods or by measuring areas of several representative leaves, averaging, and then multiplying by the total number of leaves counted.

Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation 9.4 ESTIMATION OF CROP COEFFICIENTS FROM GROUND COVER AND HEIGHT A popular and generally successful method for estimating Kc is to base the estimate on the fraction of ground covered by vegetation and the height of the vegetation. These two parameters are the primary characteristics of vegetation that control the rate of ETc act in terms of its ratio to the grass reference ET o. This method, referred to as the Allen and Pereira (A&P) approach, is explained hereafter in Equations 9.8-9.14. 9.4.1 Concepts For expanses of vegetation large enough that an equilibrium boundary layer is established, so that general one-dimensional equations such as the Penman-Monteith apply, a maximum upper limit on ET is established according to the law of conservation of energy.

text: ne-dimensional equations such as the Penman-Monteith apply, a maximum upper limit on ET is established according to the law of conservation of energy. Thus, for expanses of vegetation larger than about 500 to 2 000 m 2, the K c will have upper limits of 1.2-1.3 for the grass reference. However, under conditions of "clothesline effects" (where vegetation height exceeds that of the surroundings) or "oasis effects" (where vegetation has higher soil water availability than the surroundings), peak Kc may attain larger values. Caution is required when extrapolating ET measurements from small plots to large stands because the resulting ET may be overestimated. An upper energy-constrained limit on Kc is the maximum value for Kc (Kc max) following rain or irrigation, which is governed by the amount of energy available for evaporation.

Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation BOX 9.2 Measuring and estimating fc eff for row crops fc eff should normally represent the fraction of the soil surface that is shaded by vegetation. This value is generally larger than fc, the actual fraction of the soil surface that is covered by vegetation as observed from directly overhead. The amount of shading represents the amount of solar radiation intercepted by plants for potential conversion into evapotranspiration. The total fraction of shading is a function of the sun angle and the horizontal size and shape of individual plants (or rows) relative to their height.

text: 309 9. Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation 9.4.3 Parameterization of the ground cover fraction and height approach The application of the A&P approach requires that parameters f c, fraction of ground cover, and h, crop height, are observed or estimated from remote sensing, and that appropriate values for M L, representing the intensity of canopy shading and limitations on root and stem fluxes, and F r, the effect of increased stomatal control, are adequately selected. The parameter F r is used in the calculation of K cb full (Eqs. 9.11 and 9.12) and ML is used in the computation of the density coefficient K d (Equation 9.13). Both K d and K cb full are used when computing K cb for any crop or natural vegetation, with or without active ground cover (Equations 9.9 and 9.10).

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: Both K d and K cb full are used when computing K cb for any crop or natural vegetation, with or without active ground cover (Equations 9.9 and 9.10). It has been shown that F r plays a primary role in the estimation of Kcb and Kc, particularly for trees and vines that exercise substantial control over stomatal conductance, even under well-watered conditions. To support the application of the A&P approach for most applications to compute Kcb A&P, a selection of Fr and ML values has been performed through a numerical search of parameter values that tend to cause K cb A&P to match the tabulated K cb values in Chapter 7 (Kcb TAB). The procedure consists of: 1. Selecting initial values for F r [0.25 to 1.0] and M L [1.00 to 2.00].

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: the tabulated K cb values in Chapter 7 (Kcb TAB). The procedure consists of: 1. Selecting initial values for F r [0.25 to 1.0] and M L [1.00 to 2.00]. F r is likely to be close to 1.0 when the crop has young and very green leaves, particularly annual crops, and close to 0.50 during the late season of deciduous woody fruit crops and annual crops that are harvested dry. M L is close to 1.00 under dry crop conditions and close to 2.0 when the crop is not stressed; in addition, M L is close to 2.0 when the canopy is less transparent to radiation. Alternatively, the parameters in Tables 9.1 to 9.4 are considered. 2.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: addition, M L is close to 2.0 when the canopy is less transparent to radiation. Alternatively, the parameters in Tables 9.1 to 9.4 are considered. 2. Computing crop K cb A&P with observed/known values of f c eff and h and using the selected initial values for Fr and ML, and then comparing the resulting K cb A&P with the target value, which is commonly the standard tabulated value (Kcb target = Kcb TAB) for the same crop (Tables 7.1 to 7.3), or with a K cb target < K cb TAB when the crop is known to be cultivated somewhat far from pristine conditions. 3.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: the same crop (Tables 7.1 to 7.3), or with a K cb target < K cb TAB when the crop is known to be cultivated somewhat far from pristine conditions. 3. Repeating the computations using an iterative numerical search where the initial Fr values are progressively changed, but constrained by the limits of F r, while comparing the successive values of K cb A&P with K cb target values for the same crop, progressively decreasing the differences between both values until differences are negligible. The value for Fr needs to be progressively modified until the computed Kcb A&P effectively represents the crop under study. 4. When a F r value is selected, the calculations are performed with the F r value obtained in the previous calculation set, but now changing M L within its selected interval aiming at minimizing the difference between K cb A&P and Kcb target. 5.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: he previous calculation set, but now changing M L within its selected interval aiming at minimizing the difference between K cb A&P and Kcb target. 5. If increasing or decreasing M L leads to increases in the difference between K cb A&P and K cb TAB , then the last value for M L is retained, as well as the F r used in the calculation; however, if the difference decreases, a new run must be performed until an ML value is found that minimizes that difference. The value selected for F r in Step 3 remains fixed throughout Steps 4 and 5, but it may be required to reapply the numerical search, focusing on Fr. 6. The procedure ends when the difference K cb A&P - Kcb target is minimized and values for both ML and F r selected are within the respective intervals. These values can then be used with Eq. 9.9, 9.11, and 9.13 to calculate values for Kcb mid act for any fraction of cover.

text: 329 10. ETc act under various crop management practices ETc act under various crop management practices This chapter discusses various types of factors that may cause the values for K c act and ETc act to deviate from the standard K c and K cb values described in Chapters 6 and 7. These factors refer to the effects of surface mulches, intercropping, small areas of vegetation and estimation of K c or K cb for periods under conditions of frozen soil as well under non-active cover. This chapter is intended to serve as a resource for situations where cultivation practices are known to deviate from those assumed in Tables 6.1 to 6.4 and 7.1 to 7.3 and where estimates of Kc act and ETc act are still necessary. This chapter is by no means exhaustive; its intent is to show some of the procedures that can be used to make adjustments to Kc to account for deviations from standard conditions.

Mulches may be composed of organic plant materials, or they may consist of plastic sheets or films. 10.1.1 Plastic mulches Plastic mulches generally consist of thin sheets of polyethylene, or a similar material placed over the ground surface, especially along the plant rows. Holes are cut into the plastic film at plant spacings to allow the plant vegetation to emerge. Plastic mulches can be transparent, white, or black.

title: Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements. Second edition, revised 2025 (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 Rev.1)
text: s. Holes are cut into the plastic film at plant spacings to allow the plant vegetation to emerge. Plastic mulches can be transparent, white, or black. Colour influences albedo, mainly during the early stages of the crop. However, as the intention is to use a simple procedure for adjusting Kc for mulched crops, only generalized recommendations are given here. The published literature offers contradictory information on impacts of plastic mulches on Kc and ET. However, it appears likely that black plastic increases the soil temperature more than transparent plastic, so that transparent plastic may cause slightly smaller differences in Kc relative to not adopting any type of mulching. Plastic mulches can substantially reduce the evaporation of water from the soil surface. The impact of plastic mulch is likely more evident under trickle irrigation systems.

Associated with the reduction in evaporation, however, there may occur a general increase in transpiration from the vegetation caused by the transfer of both sensible and radiative heat from the surface of the plastic cover to adjacent vegetation. Even though the transpiration rates under mulch may increase by an average of 10-30 percent over the season as compared to no mulch, the K c values may decrease by an average of 10-30 percent due to a 30-80 percent reduction in soil evaporation.

Literature has reported differences between mulch and no-mulch K c that vary widely for the same types of crops, even for the same crops. This variability mainly relates to density of planting and cultivar and types with those producing more shading causing smaller differences. Variability is also created by measurement errors and biases. Soil texture and management impact reductions in K c since soil surface conditions may or not favour evaporation losses.

The latter vary according to the stages of development and amount of shading of the soil surface. It has been possible to reduce the wide ranges in impacts by grouping crops by stage since it is always observed that reductions in K c are greater during the initial crop stage and during the first part of the vegetative growth stage, or the pre-anthesis stages, i.e., when ground cover f c is smaller. Less mulching effect on decreasing Kc occurs by the start of mid-season since it is during that time that ground cover and fc are higher, thus allowing less solar energy to reach the soil surface.

By the end of season and during the second half of the late season, differences in the K c value slightly increase again, especially when the soil is less shaded during this period. Users are therefore advised to divide the crop season into three time-periods when estimating reductions in Kc due to mulching as indicated in Table 10.1 and 10.2. The smaller values of K c reduction often refer to black plastic mulch because it has a low albedo, thus providing more energy for soil evaporation under mulch, thus contributing to a convergence of the K c for mulched and non-mulched surfaces.
